title: Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance
abstract: Signal announced Friday that it’s limiting users’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI. Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.” “Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she said. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.” Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default. Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS. That said, users can disable this setting if they wish, which Whittaker said would “break our privacy guarantees.” She also admitted this is an “incomplete” solution, as it doesn’t “address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data.”

title: A tale of two Nvidias
abstract: Listen on Apple Podcasts Listen on Spotify We got two very different pictures of Nvidia this week, depending on whether you were focused on the company’s latest earnings report or the tech executives loudly calling for former CEO Jensen Huang’s return. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Tim De Chant, and I discussed the latest news from the AI chipmaker, which reported soaring revenue and insisted that it has no plans for Huang to return. Kirsten described this as “the tale of two Nvidias this week,” with the company’s current executives assuring investors, “Hey, we’ve got this.” At the same time, “You’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back , circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back.” (The company’s falling stock price certainly suggests that Wall Street isn’t feeling reassured.) Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. Kirsten Korosec: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China . This was coming directly from the interim CEO Colette Kress, and that coincides with the Trump administration also talking about closing off what we have discussed in the past, which is this idea of remote access — really closing and tightening all these restrictions [so] the chips can’t make it into China. What was happening is that data centers were being set up right outside, in countries like Malaysia and elsewhere, and then companies within China were remote accessing these chips, and so that’s now also been shut down. A lot is happening on the China front that is so much bigger than Nvidia, but Nvidia came out publicly and said, “Nope, we’re shutting this part down.” I’ll be very curious to see if this changes, maybe in the first half of 2027. Tim De Chant: I’d love to be a fly on the wall in some of these Trump administration conversations, because they were much more stringent in terms of export controls at the end of the first Trump administration, and that continued through the Biden administration, where they really restricted Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China. I think that something changed in the last couple of years that really opened Nvidia’s ability to sell in the country. Anthony Ha: One of the things that really surprised me as we were preparing for this episode was [learning that critics] of Nvidia’s stance towards China estimate that 20% of their business comes from China. And again, that’s not something you’re going to see directly in their financials, because that’s not direct sales to Chinese companies. But they’re saying, “A lot of the chips that are getting sold to companies in Malaysia or other companies in East Asia or Southeast Asia are going to end up [used by companies in] China eventually.” And so that could be — if Nvidia is really serious about this, I think this is something that’s very much in flux — that could actually be a pretty significant blow to their bottom line. Kirsten: Although Nvidia’s bottom line is doing just fine. In every possible way, their guidance was incredible. They beat expectations. They have a long pipeline. It was really interesting because you have that happening, and then you have all this noise happening in social media, and also a number of other tech conferences were happening this past week — Dealbook Summit, there [were] a few others in which you had the highest profile people that you can think of in the tech world commenting on Jensen [Huang], and Jensen himself commenting. So it’s like the tale of two Nvidias this week. You’ve got the earnings and the current executives really talking about, “Hey, we’ve got this.” In fact, that was the last line that Collette Kress said [on the earnings call]. And then at the exact same time, or in parallel, you’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back. So it’s really quite the drama that we are definitely not done with, by the way. Anthony: Although I think that what the folks who’d like to see Jensen Huang come back would say is that this most recent quarter is the last quarter under him. This is the [last of the] good times that we’re seeing under him. And so we don’t know how well Nvidia will do without him. It seems like Nvidia’s public stance right now [on Huang’s possible return] is, “No, that’s not happening.” But Nvidia’s public stance a week and a half before that was, “We stand behind Jensen. We have every confidence in his leadership.” So depending on the various pressures on them, you can imagine that changing. I don’t know what it would take for that to happen. I don’t necessarily think it’s that likely, but I also don’t think that just because they’re saying it’s not happening now doesn’t mean it will never happen. Kirsten: Sure, never say never. Tim: Right, never say never. I do think that to some extent, their steadfastness and how quickly they shot down the petitions asking for Jensen to return suggests there’s maybe a little bit more going on behind the scenes than we know on the outside. So that’s probably something to watch in the coming weeks. Kirsten: I think that the board is trying to be in control here, and they don’t want to be forced into a decision because someone like Elon Musk is saying that it needs to happen. And so, even if there is a day in which Jensen returns — which I think is pretty unlikely, especially because the investigation into how much and who knew what about chips being sold, allegedly, secretly to China. We don’t know the full picture of that yet. But even if they did have the full picture, they want to present control, and they definitely don’t want to appear like they have deference to some other tech billionaire out there. Tim: I’m sure they’re looking at what happened at OpenAI and not wanting to repeat that. Anthony: I imagine the dynamic’s a little bit different, since Nvidia is a public company. So, I’m not an expert on this, but I would guess it would be much harder for you Jensen Huang to come back and just toss out a bunch of board members.

title: Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages
abstract: Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work. Ask Proxy Image Credits: Ask Proxy Ask Proxy ’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website. It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party. Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy. There’s also a work-focused version, which the company explains “gets employees back to work faster, while keeping personal data off company systems.” The personal version costs $1 per day. For businesses, pricing starts at $15 per employee per month for large companies and $23 per employee per month for small teams with fewer than 49 employees. Ask Proxy works over SMS. You can text “start” to 820-732-2625. Caddy Image Credits: Caddy Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check. For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026. Comma Image Credits: Comma Comma is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished. Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies users and recommends the next steps. It can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls. Comma is free to start and open source. Fambot Image Credits: Fambot Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan. The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar. Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future. The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription. Folk Image Credits: Folk Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations. One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally. Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background. Haven Image Credits: Haven Haven distinguishes itself by presenting the concept of a “digital twin” rather than merely serving as a text-based AI assistant. According to the company, Haven understands and adapts to your preferences, routines, and decision-making styles, creating a personalized memory graph based on your interactions. As the company describes , “A personal assistant knows what you asked it to do. Haven knows what you would do and how you would do it.” Notably, the company envisions future features that customize your experiences across devices, like TV and car. Currently, Haven is available for free in beta on iPhone and Android devices, and the web. You can also reach Haven by calling or texting (435) 260-6500. Instinct Image Credits: Instinct Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion , valuing it at $10 billion. The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions. In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security .) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls . The company remains in private beta. Iris Image Credits: Iris Powered by Hermes Agent, Iris is designed to let users delegate tasks to an AI assistant directly through iMessage. Users can connect the apps they use and hand over a task with a simple message. The agent then works through the required steps, while retaining relevant context from previous interactions. It’s also designed to follow up with users proactively rather than waiting for another request. Martin Image Credits: Martin Martin is a general-purpose personal assistant reachable through SMS as well as phone, WhatsApp, email, Slack, and its own iOS app. It can help manage calendars, email, reminders, tasks, notes, and communications. It can also act on behalf of users by sending messages or making phone calls, while providing daily summaries of what needs attention. It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month.

title: Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood?
abstract: For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry . The company produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones so as not to miss the latest twist in a tawdry, cliff-hanger-happy saga. The primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions. Typically, the first 7-10 episodes of a micro-drama are free. After that, if the user wants to finish the series, they have to pay a small monthly fee which unlocks access to all of the site’s content. Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.” Lately, however, the company’s homepage is covered in AI-generated content. The reason isn’t exactly hard to figure out: the production overhead for AI content is substantially less than live-action. The profit potential, meanwhile, is substantially higher, if you can draw an audience. Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content. The project, which is wholly AI, used Avni’s face to create a digital avatar of him. In “Inevitable,” he plays himself – in a very meta plot in which he — the actor Aki Avni — licenses his face to a film studio, after which thriller-like antics ensue. This is Shortical’s first foray into such a licensing deal, but it likely won’t be their last. In a phone interview, Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project both nerveracking and exciting. “Look, it’s a new era for artists,” the actor said. “AI is a new kind of art. It’s a new format. It’s always great to be the pioneer in something.” Guy Shimoni, the CEO of Shortical, emphasized the creative potential of the new tool. “One of the things that AI does is it enables smaller teams to be able to produce these movie-scale productions,” Shimoni said. “When we were doing mobile-first live action, we were limited by budget, but now we can serve them with epic fantasies. We have kingdoms and dragons. We have superheroes. We have werewolves.” But AI-generated romances involving werewolves — who, exactly, is watching this kind of thing? Apparently, a lot of people. While China boasts the biggest microdrama audience globally, Shimoni says that most of his platform’s viewers are actually in the U.S. The industry’s viewer demographic skews heavily female . Many viewers may watch them to wind down at night , getting minor dopamine hits as they drift off to sleep. Many of the AI-generated programs that already exist on the company’s website appear to have millions of views. Now, Shortical is betting on the creation of a new generation of creators — those who, like Avni, are willing to surrender their likenesses for compensation. “ LICENSE YOUR FACE ” Shortical’s website advertises, explaining that interested parties can submit their social media handles to the company, which will then decide whether to offer them “a contract setting out the terms” of using their persona in the company’s AI-generated content. A company rep told TechCrunch that this “offering is still in its early days and hasn’t yet resulted in any signed contracts.” They added: “The series with Aki is the first time Shortical has used a real person’s likeness, and it was done through a direct agreement with him rather than through the platform. Shortical hopes the series will draw more attention to face licensing and plans to promote the offering more actively following this launch.” Much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend. Although the trend may not be a particularly profitable one for creators. A recent report in Rest of World found that Microdrama firms were paying people “between US$15 to US$700 to license their facial likenesses.” How much money is Shortical offering for its face-licensing deals? The company isn’t saying. As for if Shortical will offer royalty-based compensation for creators — like the residual system in television, “It’s a case by case [basis],” Shimoni answers vaguely. A Shortical representative further explained to TechCrunch that the company didn’t want to “share a specific figure” for Avni’s particular contract. However, the person said, he came “on as a partner in the project, and his compensation was in line with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role.” For other actors, however, the deals may be quite different. Plus, many creatives are understandably unsettled by signs of automation creeping into their industry. Until recently, microdramas seemed like a safe, entry-level gateway into the entertainment industry, where young actors could gain experience on sets and hone their craft. Now, companies are downsizing and producing content that doesn’t even require real actors. Jennifer Cooper, a longtime fan of the industry and founder of the consultancy firm Vertical Drama Love, notes that there’s a lot of distrust of AI — both from audiences and within the microdrama industry itself. “Everyone’s been impacted by AI,” she said. “A lot of us have either lost work to AI or can see that it’s devastated this industry — [taking microdramas] from something that was a rare thing in the world, that was in growth, and providing work, particularly for young people…[and now] you know, it’s been decimated.” Questions of consent with AI likenesses have also dogged the industry (some creators claim they have had their likenesses stolen ), which is something that Shortical is obviously trying to address with its new face-licensing endeavor. Yet these licensing deals could also help to gig-ify the industry, creating a scenario in which creators pay a distributor for the chance to platform their content (or their face), then receive payouts based on the audience engagement they’re allowed to generate. Shortical recently partnered with a company called Payouts.com, which describes itself as a “payout infrastructure platform powering creator and gig economy disbursements at scale.” The plan is to create a system by which creatives can seamlessly interact with Shortical’s platform and get paid. Cooper believes the push towards AI in the industry is driven by broader financial trends. Most of the microdrama business is led by startups, and VCs love to hear a growth game plan involving automation. “For anyone to get investment at the moment in microdramas, they’ve got to mention the word AI,” she says. “It’s like AI equals gold in everyone’s eyes.” Despite all the investment in this space, Cooper seems skeptical that there is actually a huge audience for this kind of content. “Some of it does get views. A lot of it doesn’t,” she said, of the AI content. “I think it’s being pushed on an audience more than there is an audience demand or wish for it.”

title: The UN fails to agree on rules regulating ‘killer robots’
abstract: Tech AI News The UN fails to agree on rules regulating ‘killer robots’ Countries agree to ‘start discussing options’ for rules around autonomous weapons. Countries agree to ‘start discussing options’ for rules around autonomous weapons. by Terrence O'Brien Nov 21, 2026, 8:03 PM UTC Photo by John Moore/Getty Images Terrence O'Brien is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths. One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called “killer robots.” Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to “start discussing options” after a largely fruitless week of negotiations. According to NPR : Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo. The compromise reached was that countries would instead have two years to propose regulations. Negotiations between countries on which regulations to adopt and how to enforce them will likely drag on well beyond that. Additionally, room was left for some of those yet-to-be-adopted regulations to remain “optional.” Humanitarian organizations and some countries see a need to urgently adopt legally binding rules as semi-autonomous weapons and drones have been responsible for a significant number of civilian deaths in conflicts around the globe, including in Ukraine , Gaza , and Sudan. According to NPR , Russia, Israel, and the US proved to be the primary obstructions: On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting’s agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons. title: Can Anthropic afford to put safety first?
abstract: Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge ’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life. The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet. The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which total roughly $900 billion over the coming years. All of these ideas sit in a fascinating tension with one another, and so Hayden and I really tried to break down how we think this might play out as Anthropic navigates the pressures of the public markets. You’ll hear us talk about the company’s unique corporate governance structure , something that is especially relevant in the wake of the ongoing Jensen Huang saga. We also get into why OpenAI seems happy to have let Anthropic go public first , and why Anthropic’s whole pitch to big customers boils down to the same safety branding that now sits in conflict with the profit-oriented part of its business. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Hayden Field, The Verge ’s senior AI reporter, on the Anthropic IPO and the economics of frontier AI. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Hayden Field, welcome back to Decoder . I’m excited to talk to you today because it’s not pure soap opera drama chaos. It’s like a normal thing that happened. It’s for once not personality-based and soap opera. It’s about cold, hard would-be cash. [Laughs] Well, there is some personality in it because we’re going to talk a lot about Anthropic’s IPO, which has a bunch of big personalities in it, and the way they have structured this company to repel the rapacious pressures of capitalism is, I would say, very eccentric. It reflects the beliefs of a number of eccentric people. Yep, absolutely. It’s really been interesting digging into the S-1 again and just seeing who was on what committee and which founders have the most control here and how much control the founders actually have, which is more than it may seem. Let’s start at the start. You and I are talking on IPO day. Anthropic is the first pure AI lab to go public. They priced the IPO at $83 a share and they got all the way up to $111. By the time people are listening to this, who knows what the price will actually be, but it’s been a real victory lap for all the people who are invested in Anthropic. A bunch of law firms have changed their homepages to be like, “Congratulations, guys!” What do you make of this? Is it just the thing that had to happen or is it a sign that the AI bubble is not going to pop? How should people think about it? I don’t think it really gives us new information about whether the AI bubble is going to pop or not, because I mean, this is peak AI hype right here. It’s the first AI lab to go public. It’s been kind of on track to break records for months. Everyone was like, “It’s probably going to beat Musk,” and then it did. I can’t wait to see his tweets later. But the other interesting part of this is that I’ve heard thousands of new millionaires and hundreds of new centimillionaires will be born from this, not to mention billionaires, too. It’s one of those things where I think the AI bubble is continuing to swell. I was even chatting with some tech workers inside a bunch of different companies this morning, and they were all saying within their companies, they’re seeing the bubble swell and swell, and they’re being tasked with doing more and more AI, even if it makes them less productive and makes the work less good. So I think there’s going to be a reckoning eventually, but right now we’re at peak AI hype and Anthropic does a great job of marketing its business as safe AI. Of course, they’re going to have more pressure around that marketing term now more than ever. So it’s going to be interesting to see the tension point kind of go into the spotlight and see how they handle this. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . I was at the Semafor conference earlier this week. I saw Sam Altman and Sarah Friar, OpenAI’s CFO, on stage there. Altman and Greg Brockman were at the DealBook conference this week. I get the sense they’re kind of happy that Anthropic went first to see what happens in the markets and to see how companies value the revenue potential of their big competitors so they can tell their IPO story better. Is that the sense you get, that Anthropic is the trial balloon? Or is OpenAI just retconning the fact that it didn’t go first? Yes, I think that’s absolutely the case. I heard there was a time in the past year that Altman was really obsessed with beating Anthropic to go public. That’s what I heard. It was all he thought about. But then with all the bad press around OpenAI this year, they’ve had setback after setback. A lot of the public is particularly focused on hating OpenAI right now. Obviously, there’s a big AI populism backlash and a lot of people hate a lot of AI, but it seems like OpenAI has really borne the brunt of a lot of public hatred and scandals this year. And so they were like, “You know what? Let’s just take a step back and let Anthropic go first.” And they seem happy to do that. Now that Anthropic has gone first and set this historic precedent, OpenAI can ride on its coattails and say, “Yeah, us too.” I doubt they would beat Anthropic’s record. Maybe they will, maybe they won’t. But either way, I think they know that things could have gone a lot worse for them if Anthropic did not go first, if it’s happening this year. I can’t stop thinking about Anthropic in terms of just dumb business fundamentals now that it’s a public company. You buy a token from them. They have to make that token for less than you pay for it. They also want to make AGI. Somewhere else they have some other huge set of costs. Just based on what we know about the business today, now that it’s a public company, are they profitable on the face of it? Do they have a long way to go before inference is so profitable it can pay for training all the new models? How does their business actually work? They have a long way to go and that is why it’s going to be so interesting to see what exactly they do here with regard to driving more revenue, which is what they’re going to have to do. I saw one estimate from Steve Rattner saying Anthropic is going to have to increase its revenue roughly 17-fold within the next 10 years to deliver a comparable return to some of its competitors in the tech industry. But even without that specific number, you can tell. I mean, when a company goes public, investors want to see a return on their investment. They want to see profits go up or just profits at all. They also want to see that even if profits aren’t a thing yet, they want to see that you’re driving so much revenue that they could see profit happening in the near term. That is something that Anthropic is going to have to reckon with more than ever before after today. I was chatting with a bunch of corporate governance experts and law professors and they were all saying Anthropic, like OpenAI, has such an unusual corporate structure that they aren’t actually beholden to shareholders in the way that some public companies are. Shareholders can never vote out executives. They don’t have a lot of power to influence anything really.

title: Chess.com’s next move is a new hub for classic games, from mahjong to sudoku
abstract: Gaming AI Entertainment Chess.com’s next move is a new hub for classic games, from mahjong to sudoku AI changed the game at Chess.com, helping it expand to 11 other classics this year.﻿ AI changed the game at Chess.com, helping it expand to 11 other classics this year.﻿ by Stevie Bonifield Nov 21, 2026, 2:00 PM UTC If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement. Image: Chess.com / Classic Games Stevie Bonifield is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI. Chess.com is ready to go a lot bigger than chess. After launching Gambit , a gambling-free poker site, earlier this year, the company is now adding 10 more games: backgammon, checkers, go, hearts, mahjong, shogi, sudoku, solitaire, xiangqi, and a Scrabble alternative called word . They’re all part of Chess’s new Classic Games platform, which is launching its public beta on Saturday on the web and through a new app for iOS and Android . “Our cofounders have had many people come up to them and say, ‘Hey, I run a mahjong night on Wednesdays’ or ‘I go to this local bar in Chicago with like five people, and we love playing go, but we lack a Chess.com,’” chief growth officer Albert Cheng says in an interview with The Verge . “The way that Chess.com has grown this community of almost 300 million members has not really happened for a lot of these other types of classic games.” Classic Games is aimed at filling that gap. Some of the new games, like shoji or xiangqi, are strategy games similar to chess while others are further afield, like sudoku, solitaire, and word . The Classic team chose the new games through “a mix of community feedback, market research, and then just our own confidence in our ability to serve that game well,” Cheng says. It’s focused on classics that “have some sort of lifelong journey of learning and a community.” Previous Next 1 / 4 Classic Games has the same bots as Chess.com, including Martin. Image: Chess.com / Classic Games Classic Games will feel familiar if you’ve ever played a match on Chess.com. Each game has lessons, leaderboards, and a rating system. Multiplayer games like checkers or mahjong have options for matches against other players or bots, and they use the same bot characters that Chess.com has. (Martin remains the lowest-rated bot across the board, whether it’s on Chess, Gambit, or Classic.) Not all of the games have the same play modes — word and mahjong have puzzles like chess, while sudoku has a set of daily grids and solitaire has daily deals. The expansion hasn’t put Chess.com itself on the back burner, according to Cheng. If anything, it’s never been better. “Chess is more and more so in the public zeitgeist than I’ve ever seen it, frankly, during my time here,” Cheng says. “Our daily active users are higher than they’ve ever been during the company’s history.” He declined to share exactly how many daily users Chess.com currently has but said the site is “doing amazingly well.” So, while the company is expanding beyond its domain name, chess remains its primary focus. “The amount of folks that are fully dedicated toward building new games is less than 1 percent of the company,” according to Cheng. Previous Next 1 / 4 Multiplayer games on Classic Games have a chat sidebar. Image: Chess.com / Classic Games AI played a key role in helping Chess.com launch 11 new games in a matter of months with a team of only a few people. Earlier this year, Cheng told The Verge his team built Gambit with the help of AI , mainly for coding tasks. He says they used “almost entirely the same approach” for Classic, with AI helping to speed up the coding process again. “Because these games are built on top of the Chess.com code base and design system and bot characters and rating systems, it’s a huge advantage and allows us to move very quickly alongside AI to bring these types of games to market with a very small team,” Cheng says. “As we create more and more games, the adjacent games that can be created to it just happen much faster because the infrastructure is there, as opposed to standing everything up from scratch.” AI wasn’t used for Classic Games’ art and design, Cheng says. “The look and feel of it is very carefully crafted by humans, and we’re proud of that,” he says. “The truth is, it really is a blend. It’s a small team of really talented folks that have good product and design judgment, and they’re leveraging AI.” “We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years.” Chess.com’s comfort with AI may come from the fact that human chess players have now spent decades playing and learning alongside machines. “We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years,” Cheng says, calling back to Garry Kasparov’s 1996 chess match against IBM’s Deep Blue supercomputer. “Even before the company was founded 20 years ago, the idea that AI was super powerful at the game of chess was embedded in how the cofounders thought about the company.” Elsewhere in the games industry, there’s been increasing tension over the use of AI . Cheng says that while Chess.com may be using AI to “accelerate” coding tasks, the creative side of things has become more important. “On the art and the design side, the ratios are shifting a decent amount, where we’re hiring more of those folks,” he says, adding that the company has “shipped a lot more major features in Chess.com than in previous years” using what they’ve learned from Classic Games’ faster development process. Chess.com might not be done growing its library of games, either. Cheng said it will likely expand to “a lot more” games in the future. title: Meet Thinking Machines Inkling 2 Mini: 26B Looped MoE Runs on a 32GB Mac
abstract: Thinking Machines Lab has released Inkling 2 Mini , an open-weight looped transformer with 26.4B total parameters. The model reuses its middle layers 3 times per token instead of adding more weights. That keeps the checkpoint near 20GB, small enough for a 32GB Mac or 1 NVIDIA DGX Spark. For developers, Inkling 2 Mini is a local option for agentic coding, tool use and document work. It ships under Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face , with hosted inference and fine-tuning on Tinker . Inkling 2 Mini is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts model from Thinking Machines that loops its middle layers. It accepts text and images and returns text only. It follows Inkling 2 Small, a 594B-parameter model released on November 5. The model stores 24 layers, grouped into 4 blocks of 6. The first and last blocks run once. The 2 middle blocks run 3 times with shared weights. That gives 48 layer applications per token from 24 layers of weights. Each pass after the first receives a “message” from the previous pass. Thinking Machines carries it with Attention Residuals and a learned gate. Feed-forward layers use 128 experts, with 8 routed per token. Looping the middle layers gave a 1.51x to 1.91x compute-equivalent gain. Looping the last layers gave only 1.24x to 1.36x. The middle-loop variant won 27 of 28 evaluations. Looping costs training compute but saves inference. An unlooped baseline used 7.5% less training compute. It needed 140% more inference compute to match the looped model’s loss on 512k-token agentic traces. Training began with 384 experts per layer, with 8 active per token. At midtraining, the team pruned two-thirds of them and kept the 128 most-used experts. A 1T-token distillation run from a larger internal Inkling model then healed the pruned model. Post-training used SFT, then RL over 2.2T tokens and 2,000 steps, plus on-policy distillation. Expert layers are trained and deployed in NVFP4. The last 4 layers use MXFP8. Thinking Machines says this removes quantization conversion loss. A research variant, TML-d24-varloop-research , trains with 1 to 5 passes. All Inkling scores below are self-reported by Thinking Machines. Coding is the strongest area. Inkling 2 Mini scores 79.2% on SWE-bench Verified (bash only) and 77.9% on SWE-bench Pro v2 (Hard). It reaches 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1, where Qwen’s own card lists Qwen3.8-27B at 42.2%. On Terminal Bench v2.1 it scores 71.6%, behind Qwen3.8-27B at 73.0%. Agentic search also holds up: 79.0% on BrowseComp with compaction and 82.7% on MCP Atlas. For documents and vision, it posts 92.8% on OmniDocBench v1.6 and 74.9% on MMMU Pro. On reasoning, it scores 86.6% on GPQA Diamond and 49.3% on ARC-AGI-2. Efficiency is the headline claim. On Stanford’s Intelligence per Watt metric, Thinking Machines reports 0.703 on a DGX Spark. It lists Qwen3.6-35B-A3B at 0.430 and Gemma-4-26B-A4B at 0.159. Each column uses the vendor’s own model card. Harnesses and settings differ, so treat cross-vendor gaps as directional. The checkpoint is about 20GB in Safetensors. Thinking Machines lists 3 supported setups: 1 NVIDIA DGX Spark, Apple silicon with 32GB+ memory, and other GPUs with 32GB+ VRAM. Quantized GGUF builds are available through Unsloth and llama.cpp. Serving support covers Transformers, vLLM, SGLang, Ollama, NVIDIA Dynamo and TokenSpeed. Tinker pricing for Mini is not disclosed in the launch materials. A vLLM quick start takes 1 command: vllm serve "thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini" . Knowledge depends mostly on total parameters, and looping did not help knowledge benchmarks. Inkling 2 Mini scores -8.6 on AA-Omniscience, with a 63.4% non-hallucination rate. It is not the best small model for multi-turn chat or constraint-heavy prompts. It scores 50.0% on MultiChallenge and 33.4% on ComplexConstraints v1.1. It also trails larger models on HLE-Diamond (15.2%) and CritPt v2. Check out the technical blog , model card , model weights and Tinker Playground . title: OpenAI Ships GPT-Live-1.1 for Voice Agents, Cuts Idle Cost to $0.02/Min
abstract: OpenAI has made GPT-Live-1.1 available in its API under the model ID gpt-live-1.1 . The GPT-Live-1.1 voice model is a full-duplex model for multilingual conversations. It can listen while it speaks. OpenAI team states that it speaks with more natural and consistent accents across languages and completes tasks more reliably. The release also adds standby, a cheaper billing state for idle sessions. For teams running voice agents, idle time on a call now costs less. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . GPT-Live-1.1 is a full-duplex speech model from OpenAI that hears and speaks in 1 stream. It follows GPT-Live-1, which reached the API on September 10, 2026 . As per the OpenAI forum announcement , it has powered ChatGPT Plus and Pro voice since October 15. Inputs and outputs are audio and text. Image and video are not supported. Streaming and function calling work. Structured outputs, fine-tuning and predicted outputs do not. The GPT-Live family replaces the usual cascade of speech-to-text, an LLM and text-to-speech. OpenAI says the model reasons over incoming and outgoing audio together in a single model . It also handles turn detection and returns ASR transcripts natively. Deeper work is delegated. The voice model can hand reasoning and tool calls to a backend text model. OpenAI names GPT-6 Astra for complex issues and Luna for high-volume tasks. Third-party backends also work. The Live conversations guide sets delegation.type to client or responses . Responses mode uses OpenAI models. Client mode connects your own backend. Instructions can run up to 16,384 tokens. OpenAI lists 4 improvement areas for 1.1: Standby pauses inference during silence while the WebRTC connection stays open. The guide documents 3 settings: After the timeout, the server emits session.paused . When the user speaks, session.resumed fires. The session ID and history are kept. OpenAI warns the first reply after a short utterance may be slower. Keep the microphone track active during standby. Standby works for both GPT-Live-1 and GPT-Live-1.1. Voice sessions are billed by duration. The GPT-Live-1 model page says billing is per second. Backend model and tool usage are billed separately. That matters: a heavy backend can cost more than the voice layer. The model is API-only. You switch an existing Live session by setting model to gpt-live-1.1 . Changing the model requires a new session. Outbound SIP calling reached all organizations on November 2, so phone agents are supported. GPT-Live-1 and GPT-Live-1.1 have separate concurrent-session limits. Each limit applies across inference regions. The 1.1 page does not publish tier numbers. title: Baseten Releases Bison-1 and Groundhog-1, Topping Decision Model Index
abstract: Baseten has released bison-1 and groundhog-1, 2 open-weight decision models built on Google’s Gemma 4 . Decision models do not write text. They return calibrated probabilities for yes/no, choice and score questions. The Baseten bison-1 decision model scores 76 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1 . That ranks #1 of 19. Both models raise context from 16k to 128k tokens and accept images. For routing, triage and guardrail pipelines, that means full policies and histories in one call. bison-1 is a 31B decision model from Baseten that post-trains Gemma 4 31B to return calibrated probabilities. groundhog-1 is the cheaper sibling. It fine-tunes Gemma 4 26B-A4B , a mixture-of-experts model with about 4B active parameters per token. Both join Baseten’s existing lineup: mammoth-1 (27B), elephant-1 (9B) and joey-1 (2B). Those 3 sit on Qwen backbones. The new pair is Baseten’s first on what it calls an American backbone. A request carries 1 state and any number of questions . The state is text, optionally with images. Each question has a type: noul (yes/no), choice (named options) or score (ordered levels). The model answers every question in a single prefill pass. It returns P(yes), or the chosen option with a probabilities field. No output tokens are generated. Baseten’s earlier launch post lists ticket triage, spam detection, jailbreak guardrails and LLM routing as target tasks. Requests longer than the trained limit are refused, not truncated. Pipelines that assume silent truncation will need a length check. Baseten credits two sources: the Gemma base and more “soft labels” in the training mix. Soft labels use probability targets instead of 1 fixed correct answer. The model learns to report uncertainty that tracks how often it is right. The result is a Brier score of 0.14, the lowest on the index. Baseten puts d1.2-ultra at 0.15. Lower is better. On AA Decision Index v2.1, bison-1 scores 76. Liquid AI’s d1.2-ultra scores 75 and mammoth-1 scores 71. The index blends 6 evaluations, led by AA-Paperclip at 30%. The bison-1 model card breaks out each component: bison-1 ranks first on 4 of 6 components. Knowledge-heavy decisions are its weak spot. On long context, Baseten reports LongMemEval M (128k) of 84.8 for bison-1 and 77.4 for groundhog-1. LongMemEval S reads 87.1 and 79.3. groundhog-1 has no official index score yet. Baseten expects it to match mammoth-1. Both models are live on Baseten Model APIs . They use the same API as the older decision models, so switching means changing 1 model name. The IDs are decision-models/baseten-bison-latest and decision-models/baseten-groundhog-latest . Pricing mirrors the older pair. bison-1 costs $0.10 per 1M tokens, like mammoth-1. groundhog-1 costs $0.035, like elephant-1. The bison-1 library page lists that as an input price, since no output tokens are produced. Open BF16 weights sit on Hugging Face. Baseten lists no inference GPU or quantized builds. Training used 192 B200 GPUs for bison-1 and 128 for groundhog-1. Check out the launch post , the bison-1 and groundhog-1 model cards, and the Baseten docs . title: New in AWS Quick: More capable flows, an updated web experience, and agents that work together
abstract: Turn one person’s process into your team’s process, get more done in the Quick web app, and get more complete answers from agents working together. AWS Quick is the AI workspace built only for work. Today, we are releasing updates that help your team get more of its everyday work done: AI assistants make individuals faster, but the gains often stay with one person. The way one analyst builds the monthly report rarely becomes the way the team builds it, and work waits until someone is back at their desk. This release helps your team turn what one person knows into a process everyone can rely on, and keeps work moving when you step away. AWS Quick Flows already helps teams automate and standardize business processes so people can focus on their most important work. Now you can build, run, and refine flows entirely in chat. And your flows can take on more of your tough work, whether you start it from the web, desktop, or mobile app. For example, here is how flows could support a finance team. Maya is a financial planning and analysis manager at a retailer. Each month, she prepares a report for her VP of Finance that explains changes to costs and margins. For each region, she pulls last month’s results, compares them to the plan in a spreadsheet, writes commentary on the biggest changes, and sends the report. The process lives in her memory and a personal checklist. When she is out, a teammate has to rebuild the report from scratch, and it looks different every time. With Quick, Maya can standardize the process, automate it, and make it available to her team. She describes her process in chat, the way she would explain it to a new employee. Quick builds the flow from her description and she tests and refines it in the same conversation. A diagram beside the chat shows each step, so she can confirm it matches how she works. Figure 1: Maya describes her monthly report in chat, and Quick builds the flow with a diagram beside it. Both views, enlarged here for visibility, appear side by side in the same Quick window A flow can now bring together agents, skills, tools, and data, and handle longer processes with more data. Fixed calculations and checks keep the results consistent, agents draft and analyze, and Maya decides what goes in the final report. On each run, her flow: Maya publishes the flow for her team. At the next month-end, she is at a planning meeting, so Jordan, an analyst on her team, runs it from chat in the Quick desktop app. There, the flow can use a spreadsheet of regional adjustments saved on his computer. Before the report goes out, Jordan reviews the draft, including why each region was flagged, asks for a few changes in chat, and approves it for the VP of Finance. When Priya joins the team, she runs the same flow at her first month-end, and the report is built the same way. While this is a fictional example, real customers tell us they’re automating complex business processes to make them more consistent and repeatable. This gives their people back valuable time to focus on more strategic work. Take Pomelo, a Latin American fintech provider powering card issuance, processing, and payment operations for customers: “At Pomelo, AWS Quick changed who gets to build solutions. Before, every analysis or automation depended on the data team. Today, people across every area explore information, make decisions, and build their own agents and flows within a unified, governed environment. Without growing our team, nearly four times as many people now work with data each month, so our data team can focus on its most complex, high-impact work. A single use case already saves us 80 hours of work per month. But the real transformation isn’t the hours we save. Quick is transforming our data and innovation culture: we’ve gone from a few people building solutions for many to an organization where everyone can create, experiment, and change the way they work. And we’re just getting started.” — Rodrigo Marini, Head of Data, Pomelo Fintech Services S.A.S. If you already use Quick in your browser, the updated web app puts the items that need your attention on the home screen as soon as you sign in. A reorganized left navigation brings agents, flows, skills, knowledge, and connectors together under Customize. It includes the agents and skills you built on desktop and ones others have shared with you. Your existing dashboards, topics, and spaces work as before, and you do not need to turn anything on. Figure 2: The feed brings the morning’s email and messages that need a reply into one view Some requests need the knowledge of more than one specialized agent. With multi-agent orchestration, the agent you ask can bring in several specialized agents at once, each working on the part it knows best. The agent then combines their work into one response. Each agent keeps its own instructions, knowledge, and context, so the people who know that work best can build and maintain it. For example, you might ask why shipping costs rose in one region. Your agent can bring in a forecasting agent built on your team’s planning data and a procurement agent built on the procurement team’s vendor contracts. You get one response that shows what each agent contributed, and you decide what to do with it. Work lives in many systems. This release adds new connectors so Quick can pull from the analytics and tools your team uses every day. Connect once, then ask in natural language. Meta ads. Create, manage, and analyze Meta ad campaigns in natural language through a connector to Meta’s ads Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. Quick combines Meta ad data with your first-party and third-party sources, and asks for your permission before it creates a campaign, changes a budget, or takes any other write action in an ad account. Try Quick free for 3 months and invite up to 10 teammates at no cost. Amplitude. Ask about product usage, customer behavior, and conversion in natural language. Quick connects to Amplitude through its MCP server, so product and marketing teams can pull behavioral insights into the dashboards, documents, and workflows they build in Quick. Connectors respect your existing permissions. Quick only shows each person what they already have access to. Quick asks before it takes any write action. Administrators choose which connectors teams can add. Whether you build a monthly report, run one your manager built, or set up Quick for your organization, Quick works the way you do. Your data stays in your environment and does not train anyone else’s models. You bring the judgment, and Quick gives your team the capacity to match its goals. These features are available today in all Regions where AWS Quick is available. To try what’s new, sign in to Quick or download Quick and get started in minutes. title: Cut self-hosted LLM cost and latency with the distributed KV caching agent skill
abstract: Customers increasingly self-host large language models (LLMs) on GPUs for control over cost, accuracy, and latency. However, self-hosting often means paying for redundant GPU work because small, isolated caches on each server can’t hold or share the growing context AI agents and chat applications resend. Consider a legal AI assistant that can accumulate hundreds of thousands of tokens of case history in each conversation. When a lawyer returns to a thread after lunch, responses from the LLM can take minutes. The GPU server that picks up the request has none of that history in its memory. So, the GPU recomputes the key-value (KV) attention states for all of those tokens, a step called prefill, before it writes a word. The same pattern slows down resumed coding agents, agentic AI assistants, and document Q&A assistants. Distributed KV caching with Amazon ElastiCache can cut self-hosted LLM inference costs by up to 40% and time to first token (TTFT) by up to 80%. Distributed KV caching extends GPU-local caches with a shared tier beside your GPU fleet so any server can reuse KV state for days across sessions, routing shifts, and server failures. “ Announcing distributed KV caching for self-hosted LLMs with Amazon ElastiCache ” dives into the technical details and the performance benchmarks. This post details the distributed KV caching skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS. With this skill, you can evaluate and set up distributed KV caching from within your coding agent in a few prompts. The skill guides the agent through checking whether your workload benefits from distributed KV caching, setting up a cache cluster for testing or production workload, and troubleshooting your LLM inference caching. The skill works with Kiro , Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and other coding agents that support Agent Skills. We walk through how the skill works with four conversations: diagnosing a slow first token, sizing and pricing the cache, setting it up, and fixing a failed transfer. The benefits for your workload depend on characteristics such as LLM models used, user traffic patterns, and prompt routing choices, and can be complex to estimate. We created the KVTrace tool to get close estimates of the benefits for your workload, from your own model and traffic before you deploy any infrastructure, at no additional charge. The skill simplifies this evaluation and the setup, and guides your coding agent through the following best practices before changing anything: These flows, from estimating benefits to setup, require the following: We gave the agent this prompt: “My vLLM fleet serves a legal assistant with 64K-token contexts on p5 instances. Returning conversations take 13 seconds for the first token because the GPU recomputes the full conversation history every turn. How do I fix this?” The agent matches the request to the skill and, in Kiro, asks for approval before loading it. The answer identifies that the latency was caused by cold prefill, and three things in the answer matter for a real deployment. First, it checks for fixes that need no new infrastructure. If you turned off prefix caching, turning it back on can speed up back-to-back turns. If the GPU prefix cache hit rate is already above 90% with session affinity, you might not need a shared KV cache. Second, it identifies constraints specific to the legal AI assistant. A shared KV cache can let one tenant tell from response times whether another tenant sent the same text. Cases that must stay isolated get separate caches, and tenants that share a cache add their own ID to the KV hash. Third, it doesn’t guess the size. It asks for the model and TP size, KV data type, replica count and routing, and how long users wait between turns. Figure 1: The diagnosis and proposed architecture for the legal assistant To size the savings, we gave the agent an example fleet of 8 p5 instances that serve 64,000-token prompts for a multi-turn retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistant. The agent looked up the GPU and cache node prices and derived the prefill rate and KV size from benchmarks. Finally, the agent recommended two cache.i8ge.48xlarge nodes for distributed KV caching. The following figure shows the agent’s summary and the inputs it used. Figure 2: The agent’s summary and inputs. It looked up both prices in the AWS price list and explains how it arrived at the recompute figure We didn’t provide a cache hit rate, which is the share of recomputed tokens the cache would serve. The agent therefore presents scenarios and recommends a KVTrace run to identify the cache hit rate. KVTrace records the KV cache events from vLLM or SGLang. It then replays them offline against a shared KV cache of each candidate size. The recorder never writes token IDs or prompt text. Traces hold block hashes and token counts. Block hashes come from token content, so pass --anonymize-key-file when your prompts are sensitive. The skill records on every GPU server for a representative window, such as a full business day. The agent also notes that freed GPU time turns into dollars only if you run fewer servers or serve more traffic on the same ones. Figure 3: The top of a KVTrace report from synthetic demo traffic. It recommends the smallest capacity that reaches 90% of the savings ceiling. We prompted the agent with: “Set up a shared L2 KV cache for LLM inference, starting from scratch.” Before it creates anything, the agent requests your confirmation to set up the suggested cache node count in your Availability Zone, at the estimated price. Once confirmed, it creates the right security group with EFA permissions, and a Valkey 9.1 cluster that uses a custom parameter group with caching eviction policies. LMCache gets its own cache user , with the password in AWS Secrets Manager . The agent prepares the GPU servers and starts one LMCache server per GPU server. Then it checks the cluster with a small test object and confirms that repeated prompts load their KV state from the cache over Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA). On a GPU fleet, the skill checks the measured L2 share against the KVTrace prediction. For the full setup with every command, see Getting started with distributed KV caching in the Amazon ElastiCache documentation. Prompt: “My LMCache server connects to the ElastiCache cluster and BLOB.RDMA_HELLO succeeds, but actual data transfers are failing. INFO largeobj shows rdma_write_errors climbing. What’s wrong?” Following the skill’s troubleshooting guide, the agent reasons from the symptom pattern and identifies the likely cause as a security group that blocks EFA traffic between its own members. It provides you commands to check and fix the rule. Figure 4: The agent explains the symptom, then gives commands to check and fix the security group You can get the distributed KV caching skill or the AWS MCP Server from the Agent Toolkit for AWS . Then describe your problem or ask your AI agent to cut costs and latency on your GPU fleet to get started. To learn more about distributed KV caching with ElastiCache and the performance benchmarks see the AWS blog . You can see getting started with the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) at Amazon ElastiCache documentation and learn more about KVTrace at the GitHub repo .

title: Introducing managed cluster extensions for observability and user management in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm
abstract: Keeping a shared Slurm cluster for foundation model development in sync entails keeping several separately maintained pieces of configuration matched to what’s running on the nodes. The cluster’s shape lives on multiple configuration files, its software in custom scripts, its network topology in files that must be edited as nodes change, and its users in a roster that an administrator must maintain and rerun. Over time these pieces drift away from what’s actually running, and nothing tells you when they do. We believe cluster configurations should be managed the way you manage the rest of your AWS infrastructure. You declare what you want through an API or the console, AWS validates it before it’s applied, the cluster is kept in that state continuously, and you can see whether it’s working. During 2026, Amazon SageMaker HyperPod brought that approach to Slurm clusters, with API-driven Slurm configuration, AMI-based configuration, continuous provisioning, automatic topology management, and deep health checks. Today, we launched cluster extensions, which bring the same approach to the software and settings on running nodes, with managed extensions for observability and user management. However, through all of it, you still keep full access to every node in your cluster, including the controller node. You can SSH in, configure nodes directly, and run your own lifecycle scripts. The APIs give you less to maintain, direct access gives you more control, and you choose the balance. In this post, we walk through the features we introduced in 2026 and explain why the software on running nodes needed a different mechanism. We then show how cluster extensions work, through both the API and the console, and follow a platform team through a quarter on a cluster that uses them. We can think of a Slurm cluster’s configuration grouped into six layers. Five of them describe the cluster itself: its definition, node setup, capacity, network topology, and hardware health. The sixth covers the software running on its nodes, which we discuss in the next section. The following figure shows the six layers. Earlier in 2026, we brought declarative management to the first five layers. With API-driven Slurm configuration , administrators define node roles, partitions, and Amazon FSx for Lustre and Amazon FSx for OpenZFS mounts in CreateCluster and UpdateCluster requests, and connect an external accounting database . HyperPod updates partition settings while preserving other controller-node Slurm customizations. AMI-based configuration replaces routine setup scripts with images preconfigured with Slurm, Docker, Enroot, Pyxis, and home directories. A custom AMI or OnInitComplete script handles organization-specific software. Continuous provisioning for Slurm retries capacity requests in the background; AMI-based configuration works with it , minimum capacity requirements let teams specify MinInstanceCount, and cluster operations track scaling requests. Automatic topology management maintains the network layout as nodes scale or are replaced. On Slurm 25.11 or later, partition-level topology supports tree or block topology per partition. For hardware health, on-demand deep health checks stress GPUs and test NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) connectivity, while deep health checks with continuous provisioning run as nodes are provisioned. Nodes under check stay in Slurm maintenance reservations until checks finish, keeping jobs off them. The five layers described so far are configurations that HyperPod can derive or apply once, when it provisions a node. The sixth layer, the software that runs on the nodes, behaves differently because it keeps changing for the life of the cluster. As researchers join and leave, a team asks for deeper GPU metrics for a week, and an exporter ships a fix. For this layer, lifecycle scripts have been the main mechanism so far, and they have drawbacks when the software keeps changing. A script runs only when a node is provisioned, so each change means editing it and then replacing nodes or rerunning it across the fleet. A mistake shows only when the script runs on a node, and nothing reports what’s installed, so nodes drift apart over time. We wanted the software to be declared in one place, checked when you submit it, kept consistent across nodes, and visible afterward. In November 2026, we launched cluster extensions, which are software packages managed by AWS that you install, configure, update, and remove through APIs or the Amazon SageMaker AI console, starting with observability and user management, including directory integration, as the first software extensions. Compared with scripts, extensions have these advantages: Use cluster extensions when HyperPod offers a managed software capability. Use custom AMIs and lifecycle scripts for organization-specific software or initialization that the available extensions don’t cover. HyperPod supports two cluster managed extensions today: The following diagram shows how an extension reaches your nodes. Figure 2: HyperPod can install, edit, or remove an extension. HyperPod records the desired configuration, a node agent applies the extension package on every node, including new and replaced ones, and health probes report status and health issues back You can use cluster extensions from the SageMaker AI console or through an API. On the console, the Extensions tab on a cluster’s details page lists each extension with its status, version, and ARN, and it’s where you install a new one. Each extension adds controls of its own, such as the metric store and an open dashboard in Grafana button for observability, and the number of users and groups and a Manage users button for user management. You can also manage every extension through APIs, from the AWS CLI or an SDK, to script installs, keep settings in version control, repeat a setup across clusters, or check status and health from your own tooling. The following table lists the six cluster extension APIs, from installing an extension to listing the versions you can upgrade to, along with console view for extensions. Figure 3: Left, the six cluster extension APIs and what each one does. Right, the console view to add and remove extensions The following diagram shows what happens after you call one of these APIs. Figure 4: You declare an extension’s version and settings through the API. HyperPod validates and records them, applies them to every node for its role, and reports status and health When you create or update an extension, HyperPod validates your settings against the version’s schema during the API call, so a misspelled setting is rejected immediately. It then records the version and settings as the desired state and applies them, with each node installing only what its role needs, such as GPU exporters on GPU nodes only. New and replacement nodes get the same state a few minutes after they start, and every node reports whether the extension applied and whether it’s healthy. Updates send only the settings that you want to change, and HyperPod merges them into the stored settings. Problems that show up only on a node, such as a port or user ID that something else already uses, appear in the Health field of DescribeClusterExtension, grouped by cause with a code, a message, and a count of affected nodes. HyperPod retries internal failures on its own, and for anything else you fix the cause and call UpdateClusterExtension with no changes to retry the affected nodes. An extension’s status is Creating or Updating while a change rolls out, Active when every node runs the requested version and settings and none reports a problem, and Degraded when some nodes failed or report a problem. Each extension has its own ARN, so a platform team can own sagemaker-user-management while a monitoring team owns sagemaker-observability.

title: GPT-6.2 Astra再次暴擊具身模型：16項任務成功率較GPT-6 Astra翻倍
abstract: GPT-6.2 Astra再次暴擊具身模型：16項任務成功率較GPT-6 Astra翻倍 衡宇 2026-11-21 14:35:59 來源： 量子位 還實現可變形物體操控全球首通 衡宇 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI GPT-6.2 Astra又給具身智慧上強度了，狠狠來了一計天馬流星拳。 機器人基礎設施公司XDOF的最新實測中，GPT-6.2Astra操控雙臂機器人 完成16項操作任務的綜合成功率 ，從兩個月前GPT-6Astra的19.6%飆升至41.2%，翻了一倍有餘。 打結、展開T恤 這兩項此前無AI通關的操作，這次也被它拿下。 公佈成績後，OpenAI Developers官方賬號轉發了這條訊息，OpenAI聯合創始人兼總裁Greg Brockman也驕傲發言： GPT-6.2 Astra在機器人技術方面表現得非常出色～～ 為確保評測嚴謹，XDOF以六臺YAM工作站並行試驗，每項任務重複三十次，單日可完成480場實測，並由人工標註子步驟、抓取失誤與碰撞，濾除硬體偏差與隨機擾動。 縱使標準如此嚴苛，XDOF也在最新推文中表示，Ember‑0基準或不久後便會被模型能力飽和。 兩個月成績翻倍，到底有多強？ 要理解這次突破的含金量，得先搞明白測試任務究竟難在哪裡。 GPT-6.2Astra參加的是XDOF推出的Ember-0測試。 這是一套面向真實物理環境的機器人評測基準，使用雙臂機器人完成16項操作任務，每項任務按照30次重複測試的協議執行。 測試覆蓋空間推理、物體抓取、雙臂協作、工具使用、精細操作和柔性物體處理等能力。 兩個月前，GPT-6Astra在Ember-0測試中的綜合任務成功率為19.6%。 到了GPT-6.2Astra，這個數字已經飆升至41.2%，增加了21.6個百分點，超過原來的兩倍——這裡的41.2%是16項共享操作任務成功率的等權平均，涵蓋物體抓取、空間推理、雙臂協作、工具使用等多種能力。 So，進步並非來自某一項任務的單點突破， GPT-6.2Astra在整套測試中的表現都有了明顯提升。 最讓人眼前一亮的當屬“ 給繩子打結”和“展開T恤這”兩項操作被GPT-6.2Astra輕鬆拿下。 此前，Ember-0累計進行了143次有效的T恤展開測試，沒有一個模型成功完成這任務來著。 除了這兩項標誌性突破外，在Ember-0涵蓋的其他多項任務中，該模型的表現也有明顯進步。 需要物理推理的“拉動毛巾取回遠處毛絨玩具”和“傾斜托盤讓球滾入碗中” 考驗記憶與感知的“尋找被遮擋馬克筆”與“遵循紅色便籤上的隱藏指令” 考驗精細力控的“不捏碎薯片並移動”“用夾子夾起麵包”和“端麥片上托盤” …… GPT-6.2 Astra在各個子任務的檢查點完成度與最終成功率上均展現出顯著提升。 提升最明顯的是用夾子夾起麵包的任務 ：GPT-6Astra的成功率只有10%，GPT-6.2Astra則提升到了90%。 為什麼打結、展開T恤這麼難？ 要理解GPT-6.2 Astra這次突破的含金量，得先搞明白“打結”和“展開T恤”這倆任務對機器人來說到底有多坑。 在機器人學習領域，以Diffusion Policy、ACT和RT-2為代表的視覺-語言-動作模型 （VLA） 及專用策略模型，通常需要依靠大量人類示教資料來學習操作技能。 人類先示範，機器人再從中學習如何抓取、移動和擺放物體。 這套方法在剛性物體和固定流程中已經取得了不錯的效果。 杯子、箱子等物體的幾何形狀相對穩定，抓取位置和運動軌跡也比較容易預測，模型經過訓練後，往往能夠形成較為穩定的操作策略。 But，換一種物體、換一個環境，或者把幾個動作串聯成更複雜的任務，原有策略就未必還能奏效。模型可能需要重新採集示教資料、補充訓練，才能適應新的操作條件。 柔性物體又把難度推高了一層。 展開T恤或給繩子打結時，物體的形態會隨著機械臂每一次接觸、抓取和拉扯不斷變化，形變過程也很難提前預測。機器人需要理解“把衣服展開”這樣的任務目標，還得從腕部和頂部攝像頭傳回的視覺畫面中，持續判斷衣物的角點、褶皺和整體形態，再決定下一步該如何動作。 這對操作精度和雙臂配合提出了很高要求。 抓取位置或動作節奏稍有差池，都可能導致衣角滑落、繩索纏繞，前面完成的操作也可能因此付諸東流。 在XDOF的評測體系中，“打結”和“展開T恤”這兩項任務對應的核心能力標籤涵蓋了形變控制、雙臂協調、精細操作 （Dexterity） 以及長程規劃 （Long horizon） 。 在沒有觸覺反饋的硬體條件下，大模型每次輸出動作塊 （Action chunk） 之間還存在十餘秒到二十餘秒的推理延遲，機械臂在等待新決策期間無法即時微調，這使得每一次接觸控制和失敗恢復的成本都極高。 因此， 打結和展開T恤考驗的是一整套綜合能力，包括三維空間理解、雙臂協同配合、精細接觸控制、基於歷史記錄的動態狀態追蹤以及長程任務規劃。 BTW，速度也是第二系統模型一直面臨的挑戰。此前，外界對這類模型的批評之一，就是推理過程耗時較長，難以滿足機器人即時操作的要求。 這次GPT-6.2Astra也在速度上有所改善。 模型釋出期間，其平均預測延遲從GPT-6Astra的15秒下降至10.1秒。 不過，與其他模型架構相比，這種推理方式的效率仍然偏低。對於需要連續感知、快速響應的機器人來說，10秒左右的等待時間依然不短。 但是總的來說，具身智慧模型往往在簡單抓取和物體擺放上表現不錯，一旦遇到複雜接觸、工具使用和柔性物體，成功率就會明顯下降。 XDOF此前公佈的Ember-0測試結果也呈現出類似問題。 比如模型通常能理解任務、規劃出看起來合理的動作，真正落到機械臂上，卻容易在抓取、接觸和連續操作環節掉鏈子。 GPT-6.2Astra這次的突破，恰好表示通用模型已經開始突破這些難點。 △ 圖片由AI生成 而從行業視角來看，通用大模型對具身智慧的衝擊，也正在沿著這條路線持續推進。 從輝達研究團隊測試GPT-6Astra直接充當機器人策略模型，到Claude在機器人模擬環境中展現複雜操作能力，再到Google DeepMind將Gemini的多模態理解能力延伸至機器人控制，通用模型正在一輪輪重新整理具身智慧的能力邊界。 One More Thing 活躍在機器人/具身智慧領域的新加坡國立大學總統青年教授Jiafei Duan隨後也發帖讚美了GPT-6.2 Astra“入侵”具身智慧的優秀表現。 在他們做的真實機器人對比測試中，GPT-6.2 Astra表現賊出彩，一天內就衝到了RoboColosseum的SO-101 Elo排名第一。 實際操作情況，請看小螢幕： 自初代模型在柔性操作前束手無策，及至GPT‑6.2 Astra兩月內實現成功率翻倍、破局多項零分任務，前沿多模態大模型在物理世界的演進步伐，正在持續加快。 而且是以讓人有些應接不暇的速度。 title: 剛剛，DeepSeek V1作者創業專案曝光：開源Agent
abstract: 剛剛，DeepSeek V1作者創業專案曝光：開源Agent Jay 2026-11-21 14:32:31 來源： 量子位 專為本地部署而生 聚是一團火，散是滿天星。 剛剛，前DeepSeek V1作者、DeepSeek-VL專案負責人 Tony Zhang ，正式公佈了自己的新創業專案： Linger 。 方向，正是當下最火的個人 Personal Agent 。 X 帖子影片.mp4 路線也是比較有意思，當同行都在做APP，他們優先選擇了電腦。 這意味著，Linger能操縱你電腦已有的網頁、郵件箱、日曆，無需折騰一大堆登入憑據。 遇到卡住的地方，你也可以直接上手接管。 X 評論影片.mp4 另外一個點，作為中間層的Linger，支援接入各個第三方模型。 並且專門為本地LLM做了最佳化。 具體來說，一塊12GB視訊記憶體的RTX 3060顯示卡，就能跑起一個125B參數的 Qwen3.8-Flash-Next ，並且 是45.5 tokens/秒的生成速度。 對了，還有個蠻重要的點—— 這套系統是開源的。。。 至於為什麼？ 在官宣帖中，Tony Zhang引用了PC崛起的歷史： 1960年代，計算是中心化的，直到PC將權力交到每個人手中。如今，AI在資料中心訓練，然後以token的形式租給你。 我們相信智慧應該是分散式的。你的上下文、你的資料，以及驅動它們的智慧，都應該完全由你擁有。 所以今天，他們開源了Linger，一個生活在你個人電腦上的專屬Agent。 也是延續大肥鯨優良傳統了😭。 一個「會主動，能自學」的AI Linger的的核心，是名為「Another Me」的Agent系統。 它首先是一個記憶中樞。 Linger會在本地讀取你的收件箱、日曆、聊天記錄和會議，每晚自動將這些資訊整理成個人知識庫 （Wiki） ，供所有Agent查詢。 在衡量長期對話記憶能力的LoCoMo基準測試中， Linger的準確率達到了95% ，超過了Mem0、MemOS等多個記憶增強型AI系統。 有了這些，Linger便能更好地主動工作。 它會默默觀察你的資訊流，根據事件的重要性和緊急性決定何時提醒你。週一收到客戶郵件，要求週五前給報價，它不會立刻打擾，而是等到週三早上再彈出提醒。 但如果是會議時間變更，它會立即通知。 這個Agent還會從你的反饋中自我學習，Linger稱之為「隱式強化」。 比如，當它提醒你一張發票快到期了，你回覆說「上週就收到了，應該當時就告訴我」。系統會記下一個線索。 如果下一次另一張發票出現類似情況，你再次表達了相同的偏好，系統就會自動生成一條規則： 「供應商發票→立即提醒」 。 反之，如果你連續兩次對「快遞提醒」表現出不感興趣 （比如直接忽略或回覆「不用告訴我」） ，它也會學會以後保持沉默。 你也可以直接下指令，一次性教會它。比如告訴它：「客戶的回覆，要立刻通知我」，或者「晚上9點後，會議變更這種事不用馬上說」。 這種持續的互動和學習，讓Agent越來越懂你的工作習慣，成為一個真正個性化的助理。 除此之外，Linger還能： 操作桌面和瀏覽器 。 就是開頭說的，Linger能直接使用你電腦上已經登入的Chrome、各種App，無需重新配置。 組建Agent團隊 。 這點就是DeepSeek之前解釋過的Super Agent原理了。 你下達一個複雜任務時，Another Me會呼叫或建立不同職能的Agent，協同完成工作。 而你，只用停留在和Linger的這一個Session。 X 評論影片.mp4 語音互動 。 這點主要就是服務於辦公場景了。 Linger能即時轉錄會議，會後直接向Agent提問會議內容，並讓它跟進待辦事項。 總而言之呢，就是一個專為辦公場景最佳化的Personal Agent。 不過，也有網友對這一產品定位不太理解： 為什麼不基於DeepSeek harness開發🤣跟ds-bot有何區別呢 對此，Tony Zhang回應道： Linger的重點是把模型和harness一起最佳化：12GB顯示卡就能本地跑125B模型，不按token付費，資料也不出本機。 從產品定位上看：DS-Bot的核心是Bot與Bot、Bot與群組的協作；Linger的核心是人與自己的Agent、Agent與本地環境。 12GB顯示卡，跑125B模型 讓消費級硬體執行千億大模型，Linger的核心技術是一個名為 PolyStrata 的MoE推理引擎。 它的原理可以理解為一種智慧分層儲存機制。 對於一個龐大的MoE （專家混合） 模型，PolyStrata會把最常用、最活躍的「專家模組」放在最快的GPU視訊記憶體裡，將不那麼常用的放在記憶體中，而使用頻率最低的則放在SSD固態硬碟上。 當模型需要呼叫某個專家時，系統會動態地在GPU、記憶體和SSD之間行動數據。這樣一來，就不需要把整個幾十上百GB的模型全部塞進有限的視訊記憶體裡。 效果立竿見影。 根據官方資料， 一個125B參數的Qwen3.8-Flash-Next模型，在一臺配備12GB RTX 3060和64GB記憶體的電腦上，可以實現45.5 tokens/秒的生成速度。 在更強的RTX 5090 （32GB） 上，速度則飆升至179 tokens/秒。 為了讓使用者更方便地用上本地大模型，Linger還做了一個「模型自動駕駛 （Model Autopilot） 」功能。 它會自動檢測你的硬體配置 （GPU、視訊記憶體、記憶體） ，然後從49個語言模型、兩種推理引擎、多種量化方案和不同上下文長度的組合中，為你推薦並安裝效能最強的模型。 根據SimplexAI的評分體系，不同配置的本地裝置可以獲得媲美主流雲端大模型的能力： 8GB顯示卡+32GB記憶體 ：得分35.4，約等於 Gemini 2.5 Pro 。 Mac 24GB統一記憶體 ：得分51.9，約等於 Claude Opus 4.5 。 12GB顯示卡+32GB記憶體 ：得分57.3，約等於 Claude Opus 4.6 。 這意味著，你的遊戲本或MacBook，將擁有一個真正強大的、7×24小時待命、沒有token費用、並且資料完全不出本地的AI大腦。 DeepSeek-VL負責人再創業 Linger背後，是一支有著深厚技術背景的團隊，其創始人Tony Zhang的履歷尤為亮眼。 （畢竟是DeepSeek系嘛…） Tony Zhang本科畢業於浙江大學，2019年在香港科技大學取得博士學位，隨後加入 微軟亞洲研究院 （MSRA） ，長期從事計算機視覺和生成模型研究，是VQ-Diffusion、Rodin 3D數字人等多個知名專案的作者。 2023年，他加入 DeepSeek ，擔任AI科學家。 在這裡，他不僅參與了早期語言模型 DeepSeek LLM V1系列 的研發，更是視覺語言大模型 DeepSeek-VL的專案負責人 （Project Lead）
