title: 姚順雨和混元團隊上Reddit答網友，Hy小模型已進路線圖
abstract: 姚順雨和混元團隊上Reddit答網友，Hy小模型已進路線圖 衡宇 2026-11-21 14:30:55 來源： 量子位 還透露了不少訓練背後的秘訣 聽雨 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI Hy小模型已經在路線圖上，面向24GB視訊記憶體的模型也有計劃。 今天凌晨， 姚順雨和騰訊混元團隊 來到Reddit社群，圍繞剛釋出的Hy4和Hy4 flash做了一場AMA。 AMA是「Ask Me Anything」的縮寫，意思是「有什麼想問的，儘管問」。網友在評論區提問，混元團隊成員直接回帖。 參與名單上只列了Reddit賬號，至於哪個馬甲是姚順雨，我們還沒對上號…… 這場AMA的主角，是混元本月接連發布的兩款模型。 11月4日釋出的 Hy4 是旗艦，能理解文本、影像和影片，適合長程軟體工程這類需要多步推理、反覆呼叫工具的複雜任務。 11月16日釋出的 Hy4 flash ，主打日常辦公的速度和成本。它支援圖文輸入和最長100萬Token的上下文，每個Token啟用約120億參數。 Hy4和Hy4 flash都已接入騰訊WorkBuddy。混元團隊還把WorkBuddy裡的修表、改文件、做PPT等典型任務納入了內部評測WorkIndex，按這套評測測算，Hy4 flash的平均單任務成本約為旗艦Hy4的1/20。 兩款模型的權重都已公開。到了AMA，有網友直接報出自己的電腦配置： 96GB視訊記憶體、128GB記憶體，能跑Flash嗎？ 團隊說能跑，主要權重留在GPU上，部分專家層和Engram查表模組可以挪到系統記憶體。 也有人問llama.cpp，團隊說適配正在做。 聊到研發，團隊還透露了不少訓練背後的秘訣。 Flash的啟用參數還能不能減？他們拿做過的MoE稀疏度實驗解釋取捨。 讓Agent自己解題，訓練時遇到過什麼麻煩？有時它會直接上網找現成答案，跳過解題過程。 還有網友問，後訓練裡最難改善的行為是什麼，團隊只回了一個詞， Overthinking，過度思考。 旗艦Hy4的推理鏈有時偏長。到了Flash，團隊先從旗艦蒸餾，再用強化學習把推理鏈壓短。 從模型怎麼訓，到開發者能不能把它跑起來，這場AMA聊了不少平時在模型卡上只有一行、到了真用時卻繞不開的問題。 以下是AMA問答節選，按主題編排，中文譯文有刪節。 Enjoy～ Hy4為什麼「想太久」，Flash又是怎麼訓練的？ 網友： 和Hy4 preview一樣，Hy4正式版有時也會推理太久。這和強化學習的獎勵設計有關，還是和訓練資料的分佈有關？模型能學會什麼時候停下來嗎？ 混元團隊： Hy4的目標是儘量提高智慧水平，推理鏈偏長是我們知道的問題。我們可以把Hy4蒸餾成成本效率更高的Hy4 flash，並在Flash上用強化學習縮短推理鏈。 網友： 後訓練階段，最難改善的是哪種模型行為？ 混元團隊： 過度思考。 網友： Hy4現在的參數規模還有多少提升空間？以後想做出更強的模型，必須繼續加參數嗎？ 混元團隊： 我們認為Hy4還有相當大的提升空間，尤其是在後訓練上。我們在投入大規模強化學習，也在繼續改善使用者體驗和模型安全性。同時，我們計劃訓練更大規模的模型。 網友： 訓練Hy4和Hy4 flash做長程Agent任務時，多輪強化學習裡最難處理的情況是什麼？ 混元團隊： 最棘手的是訓練環境設計有漏洞，模型會鑽空子拿獎勵。比如，我們得防止Agent直接上網搜現成答案，讓它自己把任務做完。 網友： 做命令列任務時，模型編錯一個參數就可能讓命令出錯。你們怎麼提高工具呼叫的準確性，又怎麼讓模型在長任務裡記住前文？ 混元團隊： 我們在強化學習資料里加入了模型容易犯錯的難例，獎勵也做得更細，關鍵細節出錯會扣得更重。對於長任務，我們在持續拉長強化學習訓練所用的上下文，也在提升模型壓縮上下文、保留關鍵資訊的能力。 網友： 姚順雨經常提到，選訓練資料需要有判斷力。你們怎麼判斷一批資料好不好？ 混元團隊： 資料質量有很多維度，不同領域、不同任務的要求也不一樣。無論用人類專家還是智慧體，設計和清洗資料都要花很多功夫。最後還是要做實驗，看這批資料能不能帶來提升。 網友： HyRA 2.0實驗裡，Hy4帶來的提升主要來自哪裡？它有發現新的架構或資料配比方面的改進嗎？ 混元團隊： 這次提升主要來自底層吞吐最佳化。要讓模型進一步參與研發，還得提高它判斷訓練方案的能力。用AI做AI研發，本身也是一件週期長、難點多的事。 網友： 你們已經用Hy4和HyRA 2.0改進了訓練基礎設施，也訓練出了更好的小模型。接下來會做什麼實驗，看看這一輪訓練出的模型能否在下一輪更擅長做研發？ 混元團隊： 我們正在做HyRA 3.0，敬請期待。 網友： 如果讓Hy4自己執行，它現在能通過遞迴自我改進做出下一代模型嗎？你們怎麼評估這種能力？ 混元團隊： 我們的遞迴自我改進能力還處於早期，已經做了幾項內部基準，用來評估其中的關鍵能力。 Flash的參數花在哪兒了？ 網友： 不算Engram，Hy4 flash主幹約有1560億參數，每個Token啟用約120億。如果總參數不變，把啟用參數降到80億或50億，效果會掉多少？ 混元團隊： 我們做過不同MoE稀疏度的規模實驗。固定啟用參數量時，提高稀疏度能改善計算效率。但如果固定總參數，再把啟用量降到80億或50億，我預計模型質量會明顯下降。啟用參數量決定了每個Token能用多少計算，提高稀疏度能彌補一部分。 網友： Hy4 flash為什麼給Engram分配約635億參數？這個比例是怎麼定的？ 混元團隊： 我們的實驗看到了一條U形曲線。把Engram也計入總參數量，Engram佔比在三分之一左右時，接近實驗裡的最優點。佔比再往下調，計算效率會降低。 網友： Flash為什麼選擇滑動視窗注意力 （SWA） ？ 混元團隊： 滑動視窗注意力能把KV快取壓到原來的約四分之一，顯著降低部署成本。 小模型、本地部署和下一步 網友： 會有Hy4 mini嗎？還有人想要比Flash更輕的版本，跑文件解析、分類和簡單自動化。 混元團隊： Hy小模型已經在路線圖上。 網友： 下一代Hy模型會做到1.5萬億至2萬億參數嗎？ 混元團隊： 下一代Hy模型的規模肯定會進一步顯著擴大。 網友： 會考慮推出更輕量的Flash-Lite嗎？比如用來做文件解析、分類和簡單自動化。 混元團隊： 有的，敬請期待Flash-Lite。 網友： 有面向24GB視訊記憶體的模型計劃嗎？ 混元團隊： 有，未來會發布。 網友： 我有96GB視訊記憶體、128GB系統記憶體，能跑Hy4 flash嗎？ 混元團隊： 可以。主要權重和注意力計算放在GPU上，部分專家層可以卸載到系統記憶體，Engram表也可以放在記憶體裡。 網友： 同一個工作任務，託管版Hy4 flash在我的測試裡全對，本地NVFP4版本卻出現了約8%的錯誤。這個模型更難量化嗎？ 混元團隊： 量化質量很看方法和校準方式。團隊建議試試用GPTQ量化的NVFP4版本。在我們的評測裡，這個版本與BF16的差距較小，更適合這類對準確率敏感的任務。 網友： llama.cpp支援會怎麼推進？你們會和推理框架社群提前合作嗎？ 混元團隊： 我們正在做llama.cpp適配，預計近期會在社群放出。我們也在和vLLM、SGLang等社群合作。 網友： 現有的Hy4 flash還會更新嗎？ 混元團隊： 會。我們正在最佳化Flash級模型的預訓練和後訓練方案。 怎麼看模型的表現 網友： 為什麼沒公佈GPQA Diamond、τ-bench、IFBench、SWE-bench這些常見評測的成績？ 混元團隊： 我們展示的是Agents’ Last Exam、ProgramBench這類較新、難度更高的評測。你提到的幾項出現得更早，分數已經接近飽和。 網友： 我感覺有些模型的寫作能力在退步。是因為拿太多程式碼來訓練、過擬合了，還是有別的原因？ 混元團隊： 我們也注意到了，可能和訓練目標有關。我們希望模型寫得更像人、少一點套話，這方面正在改進。 One More Thing 那麼，QA實錄到這裡就結束了。 想自己試試Hy4 flash？開啟WorkBuddy，在模型列表裡選中 Hy4 flash ，把手邊待改的表格或待整理的會議紀要交給它跑一遍。 title: 米哈遊發了個VLA論文
abstract: 米哈遊發了個VLA論文 衡宇 2026-11-21 00:25:26 來源： 量子位 8B參數，50小時自主執行 henry 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 米哈遊，您是準備親自下場研究“官方指令碼”了？ （doge） 就在米哈遊崩壞AI研發團隊最新發布的研究 Gamer 中—— 你敢信，AI竟然自己玩起了《崩壞：星穹鐵道》。 鍵盤滑鼠交給AI，上來就能和可可利亞打上一架。 碰上場景機關，也能自己上手。走到“氣泡彈珠”前啟動裝置，把自己彈到另一片區域，落地接著跑。 跟著NPC跑圖同樣可以，流螢在前面帶路，AI就在後面跟著，上樓梯、拐彎，一路跑到廣場。 我勒個乖乖，這打Boss、開機關、跟人跑圖，都讓AI學會了。 這以後充值頁面裡，會不會有個“AI代肝”選項？ （注：《崩壞：星穹鐵道》是米哈遊開發的一款銀河冒險題材的回合制角色扮演遊戲。玩家乘坐星穹列車探索不同世界，通過跑圖、對話和解謎推進劇情，並組建角色隊伍進行回合制戰鬥。） VLA代肝，不燒心 咱言歸正傳，米哈遊給Gamer的定位，是面向長流程、即時互動的 通用視覺—語言—動作 （VLA） 基礎模型。 上面演示玩《崩鐵》的主力版本，由團隊基於參數量80億的 Qwen3-VL-8B 進一步訓練而來。 它能根據遊戲畫面和任務，決定按哪些鍵、滑鼠往哪裡移動、什麼時候點選，再把這些操作真正執行出來。 換句話說，螢幕畫面是它接收的視覺訊號，任務指令告訴它要做什麼，鍵鼠操作則是它輸出的動作。 相較於以往的AI玩遊戲，Gamer這次最大的亮點是 把跨遊戲的即時操作與長流程的記憶、規劃，接進同一套VLA框架。 實戰時，模型完全依靠螢幕畫面、任務指令和已有記憶做判斷， 無需讀取遊戲內部介面或底層狀態。 隨著任務推進，它還會動態記錄“剛才完成了什麼”、“下一步準備幹什麼”。 在論文中，研究還給出了一組硬核的實測資料：在覆蓋五個主線篇章、總計約50小時的《崩鐵》長流程評估中，Gamer的自主執行時間佔比超過了95%。 而為了實現這一效果，研究設計了一套三階段訓練流程： 先用跨遊戲資料練操作，再用任務示範補上思考和記憶，最後讓模型進入遊戲，通過試錯和反饋繼續提升。 首先，是持續預訓練 （Continued Pre-Training，CPT） ，讓已經具備圖文理解能力的基座模型，進一步學會操作遊戲。 具體來說，團隊把不同遊戲的錄屏與玩家操作對齊，讓模型學習畫面和動作之間的關係：人物往前走，場景會怎樣變化；滑鼠往右移，鏡頭會轉向哪裡。 這些操作被整理成統一的鍵鼠格式，讓不同遊戲的資料可以進入同一套訓練流程。 執行時，Gamer每隔200毫秒讀取一次畫面，一次安排隨後六個動作塊，每個約33毫秒，對應30Hz的控制節奏。 相當於看一眼，安排接下來一小段動作，再根據新畫面繼續調整。 其次，在微調階段，團隊整理了約1000小時高質量《崩鐵》演示，把目標分成具體操作、階段性小目標和完整任務，教模型將動作組織起來。 值得一提的是，這裡有兩個極其實用的工程設計，核心目的都是解決長流程中的推理延遲與上下文爆炸問題： – 稀疏思考”機制： 沿著確定的路線前進，可以直接操作；遇到路線失敗、目標切換或者新的互動提示，再展開推理。 – 記憶摘要機制： 舊記錄即將移出上下文時，模型先記下任務進度、失敗嘗試、重要地點和後續計劃，讓接下來的操作有據可循。 -“稀疏思考”：沿著確定的路線前進，可以直接操作；遇到路線失敗、目標切換或者新的互動提示，再展開推理。 最後，在線上強化學習階段，團隊提出TA-GRPO，把長流程拆成由記憶銜接的片段，比較不同嘗試在相應階段的表現，再利用遊戲環境核驗的結果更新模型。 比如，有沒有到達目標地點、有沒有完成當前任務，都能成為訓練反饋，訓練後臺則負責初始化和核驗。 此外，配套的 Streaming-vLLM 推理引擎還能複用已處理的上下文，並提前吐出生成且核驗完畢的動作塊，讓遊戲畫面先動起來，大幅壓低操作延遲。 實驗測試 在跨遊戲實驗中，團隊測試了Gamer的CPT版本，涵蓋《我的世界》、基於《毀滅戰士》的ViZDoom，以及OmniGameArena和GameWorld等多個遊戲環境。 比如在《我的世界》裡，它能自己轉視角鎖定史萊姆，追上去揮劍劈砍： 切到第一人稱射擊遊戲ViZDoom，它又能迅速拉槍瞄準，連續點射逼近的敵人： 此外，在上述四項公共基準上，Gamer-8B-CPT的平均得分為29.5，所列通用模型對照中，最高為僅17.6。 而在七類小遊戲、共40個未參與訓練的任務中，基座模型僅有 3.2%，經過CPT升至15.0%，SFT後提升至39.2%，加入強化學習後更是達到了49.7%—— 作為對比，同場競技的通用模型最高分 （GPT-6.1-Sol） 僅為 17.1%。 這些結果支援了團隊的核心判斷： 通過統一的鍵鼠介面，把跨遊戲學習、長期記憶和即時操作結合起來，可以讓AI在複雜遊戲中持續執行任務，並通過互動繼續改進。 團隊也在論文結尾指出，這類能力有望用於自動化測試、加快遊戲迭代，並支援新的玩法機制，從而降低開發成本。 遊戲成為AI的練習場，練出來的AI，又能反過來幫助開發遊戲。 團隊介紹 最後，我們來認識一下這項研究背後的團隊。 論文貢獻者名單共列出了8位共同一作，其中5位在米哈遊實習期間參與了該專案的研發： Run Luo： 新加坡國立大學電腦科學博士生，曾參與GUI-R1、OpenOmni等專案，在Gamer中負責三階段訓練、資料、基礎設施及評測建設。 張寬 （Kuan Zhang） ： 清華大學人工智慧學院博士生，GameScaling與GameVerse共同一作，主要負責持續預訓練、資料及評測建設。 值得一提的是，他在個人主頁中寫道，他是英雄聯盟的大師段位玩家。 Qi Deng： 米哈遊崩壞AI研發團隊成員，負責強化學習、訓推基礎設施，以及資料與評測建設。 Yukun Chen： 中國科學院大學研究生，GameScaling共同一作、多模態推理研究RuCL一作，主要負責監督微調、資料及評測建設。 Zhihao Yang： 中國科學院大學計算機專業博士生 （本科畢業於同濟大學） ，主攻遊戲與智慧體方向，在專案中負責強化學習、資料及評測建設。 Yufei Zhang： 米哈遊崩壞AI研發團隊成員，主要負責訓練與推理基礎設施建設。 Renrong Hu： 米哈遊崩壞AI研發團隊成員，主要負責基準 （Benchmark） 建設與評測。 Yi Zhang： 來自中國科學技術大學，在米哈遊實習期間參與專案，主要負責基準建設與評測。 （其他論文貢獻者可參考論文主頁） 而將視角拉遠，這支米哈遊崩壞AI研發團隊的佈局已覆蓋AI NPC、遊戲智慧體與研發自動化三大方向，持續探索大模型在遊戲體驗革新與工業化管線中的落地。 論文指導者之一鄭銀河，正是《崩壞》系列AI NPC與Gameplay技術團隊的負責人。 此前，鄭銀河曾在雲棲大會上披露過《崩鐵》的AI帕姆，以及賦能內部研發的Agent平臺EchoX。 而在學術方面，該團隊還聯合高校推出了GameScaling和Video-Arena，分別探明跨遊戲持續預訓練的Scaling Law，以及模型對動態遊戲畫面的理解邊界。 參考連結 [1]https://arxiv.org/html/2611.18397v1 [2]https://mihoyo-gamer.github.io/ 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 VLA 米哈遊 title: 黎曼猜想被證明？！Claude加持，34歲數學家放出Lean證明
abstract: 黎曼猜想被證明？！Claude加持，34歲數學家放出Lean證明 衡宇 2026-11-21 00:07:39 來源： 量子位 衡宇 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 剛剛，34歲的Anthropic數學家Levent Alpöge放出一份PDF文件， 聲稱自己與Claude合作，找到了黎曼猜想 （數學界最有名、懸賞100萬美元的百年難題） 的證明。 Alpöge沒有發表完整論文，選擇公佈了整套Lean形式化證明程式碼，分成14個壓縮檔案供外界下載。 如果把它轉成一份包含全部細節的文件，篇幅會超過25萬頁。 Alpöge還在文件裡表示， 研究到了最後階段，Claude已經遠遠跑在了自己前面 ，連他本人都表示自己“在尚未掌握證明周邊大量數學知識的情況下，就已經向外界展示了完整論證”。 原文的形容頗為生動： No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line. 臨近答案的終局，Claude不再緩步求索，它振翅騰空，以起舞完成這場奔赴。 按照Levent Alpöge的說法，這套方法還能夠解決廣義黎曼猜想 （GRH） ，並有望延伸到擴展黎曼猜想。 從1859年提出至今，黎曼猜想這道題已經懸而未決167年。多少數學家前赴後繼，至今沒人能交出完整答卷。 一場可能改寫數學史的AI研究，正在等待驗證。 （黎曼猜想是啥？可戳這篇文章速覽：《百年黎曼猜想被Claude破了新紀錄》） Claude給出了關鍵思路 Levent Alpöge給出的名為《Remark》的PDF僅有4頁。 具體到解決黎曼猜想的數學方法上，這次證明思路借鑑了函式域中解決黎曼猜想類比命題的Stepanov方法。 在函式域裡，數學家可以通過構造具有高重數零點的輔助函式推進證明。但將這套方法遷移到普通整數領域時，遇到了一個難題——整數沒有與函式求導完全對應的自然結構。 Levent Alpöge在文件裡表示，自己引導雙方找到了一個合適的數學情境，之後Claude開始展現出令他驚歎的技術能力。 期間，Claude提出了一個新的、關鍵的建議。 通過連續的Theta Lifts （Theta提升） ，在自守形式框架下逐步累積所需要的重數。 按照文件的描述，每一次提升都能增加一個單位的重數，最終形成一條足夠長的提升鏈。 Claude 還提出了一個關鍵參數： 即對於長度為X的von Mangoldt求和，Theta提升鏈的長度應當達到√X。 除此之外，整套論證涉及了相對跡公式、Iwasawa理論、Bessel週期等多個現代數論工具。 這也是作者感到驚訝的地方—— Levent Alpöge表示，自己從學生時代起就計劃用幾十年時間研究黎曼猜想，因此一直在積累可能用得上的數學工具。 Alpöge表示，自己原本以為已經為黎曼猜想準備了足夠多的數學工具，真正開始推導後才發現，整套證明調動的數學知識遠超學生時代的想像。 過去幾個月，他與Claude展開了大量合作。他對高秩自守形式領域的掌握也有限，Claude在其中展現出的技術能力令他驚歎。 當逼近問題的終點時，Claude已經跳出了常規的推理範式。 以及，在4頁文件中，作者還公開表示從OpenAI團隊中參與各類數學成果研究的人員的出色思路中獲益良多。 先扔出14份Lean程式碼 和此前在數學界引發軒然大波的那些“數學家和AI合作”case一樣，作者也沒有發表完整的數學論文。 他說，自己還沒有完全掌握這套證明周邊的大量數學知識，不適合直接向外界提交一份自己都還沒充分理解的、龐大而難讀的數學論文。 因此他選擇先公佈形式化證明程式碼。 整套程式碼使用Lean語言編寫，被拆分成14個壓縮分卷檔案，供外界下載和檢驗。 Lean是一種互動式定理證明器，可以把數學定理和推導過程轉化為機器能夠檢查的形式。 粗略理解，就是數學家把證明過程寫成程式碼，由Lean核心檢查每一步邏輯推導是否符合規則。 所以如果一套證明能夠在Lean中完整通過檢查，並且最終證明的命題確實對應原始數學猜想，那麼它就能為證明的正確性提供非常強的保障。 作者聲稱自己與Claude已經完成了整個論證的形式化，而且沒有依賴額外假設。 至於為什麼沒有同步公佈一篇完整論文，文件給出的解釋是，整個論證實在太長，目前還沒有整理成方便數學家閱讀的形式。 作者希望接下來繼續理解這套證明，尋找其中可以簡化的部分，並最終將其完整寫出來。 不過要注意， Lean能夠驗證形式化系統中的邏輯推導，卻無法自動保證研究者輸入的定理定義準確對應黎曼猜想。 因此，外部研究者還需要檢查程式碼能否完整編譯、使用了哪些公理，以及最終定理是否真的等價於黎曼猜想。 認識一下作者Levent Alpöge Levent Alpöge （萊文特·阿爾珀格） 是一位土耳其裔美國數學家，1992年出生，主要研究領域是數論 （Number Theory） 和算術統計學 （Arithmetic Statistics） 。 他本科就讀於哈佛大學，拿到滿績4.0/4.0，以最高榮譽畢業；之後在普林斯頓大學攻讀博士，導師是2014年菲爾茲獎得主、數論大牛Manjul Bhargava。 博士畢業後，他先後在哥倫比亞大學、哈佛大學開展博士後研究，併入選哈佛學會青年研究員 （Junior Fellow） 。 離開哈佛數學系的學術崗位後，他加入Anthropic，擔任Member of Technical Staff （技術研究員） ，目前主要探索大模型在前沿數學證明中的應用。 Claude此前已經把黎曼猜想推進了一大步 這並非Anthropic第一次讓Claude挑戰黎曼猜想。 今年8月，Anthropic曾公開過一項相關研究，表示公司內部一位非數學專業員工Jarred Sumner讓Claude嘗試直接攻克黎曼猜想。 雖然最終沒有成功證明猜想，但將已知能夠證明位於黎曼ζ函式臨界線上的非平凡零點中，能夠證明位於臨界線上的比例下界從41.6%提高到67.2%。 隨後，Anthropic數學家Levent Alpöge和Ralph Furman對研究結果進行了分析和驗證，並發表了相關論文。 眼尖的你一定發現了，驗證8月新成果的數學家，就是今天釋出PDF文件的Levent Alpöge…… PDF連結 https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com 相關Lean檔案分為14個壓縮包，連結依次為 title: 美國AI音樂巨頭進軍影片生成，底層模型來自中國MiniMax
abstract: 美國AI音樂巨頭進軍影片生成，底層模型來自中國MiniMax 量子位的朋友們 2026-11-20 20:18:01 來源： 量子位 美國AI音樂平臺Suno宣佈推出視覺創作工具Visuals 近期，美國AI音樂平臺Suno宣佈推出視覺創作工具Visuals，將影片和影像生成引入音樂創作流程。Suno官方披露，Visuals採用的模型名為H3 Move，基於中國AI公司MiniMax的開源影片模型H3打造，並針對音樂創作場景調優。 Suno首席產品官Jack Brody表示，Suno團隊使用自己的資料對這一開源模型進行了最佳化，使其更適合音樂影片製作。MiniMax H3提供底層模型基礎，Suno則在此基礎上進行音樂場景適配和產品整合，將歌曲創作、畫面生成與人物口型同步納入同一創作流程。 據Suno介紹，Visuals生成的影片能夠呼應歌曲結構和歌詞，並支援演唱口型同步。使用者可以選擇平臺提供的原創角色，或上傳參考圖片，結合音樂和文字提示生成最長15秒的影片片段，再通過時間軸延長、編排和編輯片段。此外，使用者還可以製作歌詞影片和專輯封面，自定義歌詞字型與顏色，並根據釋出需求選擇畫面比例。 影片創作一直是Suno產品拓展的方向，但過去生成速度較慢、成本較高，限制了普通使用者的使用。Brody表示，影片模型在速度、成本和質量上已具備向普通使用者提供影片創作服務的條件。 作為H3 Move的基礎模型，MiniMax H3於今年8月開放模型權重，支援企業和開發者在其基礎上開展部署、微調和定製。H3能夠統一理解文本、影像、影片和音訊構成的上下文，生成帶有原生立體聲音訊的影片，最高支援2K解析度和15秒時長。 結合此次Suno的創新產品形態看，這類跨模態能力與音樂影片的創作需求天然契合。H3 Move呈現了基座影片模型與垂直應用結合的一種路徑，以基礎模型的多模態生成能力為支撐，再圍繞音樂內容加入場景最佳化、編輯功能和內容保護機制。 Visuals採用獨立的付費積分體系。影片和圖片生成消耗Visual credits，與歌曲生成積分分開計費。 在內容保護方面，Suno表示，Visuals加入了文本與視覺過濾機制，針對特定藝人、公眾人物形象及受版權保護內容設定限制，並將在生成內容對外分享前嵌入水印。據Suno官網披露，已有超過1億人使用其平臺創作音樂。 本文由MiniMax提供，量子位獲授權轉載，觀點歸原作者所有。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 MiniMax 量子位的朋友們 新浪新聞·2026探索大會在京舉行 虛實交融共探智慧時代共生新圖景 2026-11-20 影視颶風、Manus、影石、OPPO……極客公園創新大會 2027 嘉賓陣容更新！ 2026-11-19 SenseNova U1 Pro獲Design Arena雙榜中國第一、全球第六 2026-11-19 AI基建大潮方興未艾，聯想集團最佳財季誕生！ 2026-11-19 相關閱讀

title: 給萬卡國產芯裝個“超級外掛”！清華團隊要造最強國產Token工廠
abstract: 給萬卡國產芯裝個“超級外掛”！清華團隊要造最強國產Token工廠 傑西卡 2026-11-20 16:59:15 來源： 量子位 聯合華為昇騰，五年衝刺十萬卡 傑西卡 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 兩年半，增長5000倍。 這是中國日均Token呼叫量的增長規模。2024年初，這一呼叫量還是1000億；到2026年6月時，已達到約500萬億。 Agent應用深入千行百業，模型能力不斷突破，AI對算力的需求正在以前所未有的速度擴張。 需求井噴之時，供給側卻面臨另一番景象。 由於眾所周知的外部環境，非國產先進算力供應的不確定性持續存在，國產晶片正加速走向主場。市場研究機構TrendForce預測，2026年中國高階AI晶片市場中，國產方案的出貨份額將 接近90% 。 毋庸置疑的一點是， 國芯國模，正在從重要的技術選擇，成為中國AI產業必須掌握的基礎能力 。 但這條主線上依然佈滿障礙。不同廠商的晶片對應不同的軟體棧，模型適配與開發者生態仍在完善；裝置上架後難以匹配真實流量，算力利用率不足…… 更深層的矛盾在於，供給側按卡數、機櫃和峰值算力衡量資源，需求側卻按照有效Token產出、響應速度和服務質量採購。 供需兩端，說著兩種不同的語言。 一家出身清華系的AI基礎設施企業—— 清昴智慧 ，正嘗試成為這中間的“翻譯官”。 11月17日，清昴聯合華為昇騰生態及多家產業夥伴，正式發起 昇騰950DT萬卡級Token工廠聯合運營計劃 。 按照計劃，清昴將以打造 國內規模最大的獨立國產Token工廠為目標 ，將分散、異構的國產算力組織起來，通過RSI驅動的軟體技術和運營體系，轉化為 可計量、可驗收、穩定交付的Token產能 。 未來五年，清昴還會進一步建設覆蓋多地域、多晶片的十萬卡級Token工廠網路，讓國產晶片真正成為支撐大模型與Agent持續執行的生產力。 萬卡計劃背後，國產AI產業正在孕育一場新的分工。 讓分散的國產算力，匯成萬卡級Token工廠 建設萬卡級算力叢集，解決的是 計算資源的規模問題 。而要讓這些算力成為一座持續生產、穩定交付Token的工廠，還需要更完整的技術與運營體系。 除了晶片、機房和電力，Token的生產還涉及 模型適配、資源排程和真實業務需求 。這些能力和資源，通常分散在產業鏈上的不同企業手中。 清昴此次萬卡計劃的特殊之處，就在於 “聯合運營” 四個字。 按照最新公佈的路線圖，清昴計劃於 2027年 推進昇騰950DT萬卡級聯合運營，建設 國內領先的獨立國產Token工廠 。 他們還計劃，未來五年，將這套體系擴展為 十萬卡級別 自主可控的Token工廠網路，實現多地域、多晶片的統一排程與全國產算力供需匹配。 面對如此龐大的算力規模，清昴選擇讓不同企業各展所長，共同參與Token生產。 具體而言，這一計劃將由四方共建、聯合運營： 華為昇騰生態提供晶片、超節點產品及技術協同； IDC和智算中心提供機房、電力與算力資源； 模型與流量方提供真實業務需求，並參與服務質量驗收； 清昴智慧作為生態組織者，承擔中間的軟體最佳化、叢集排程、統一計量和聯合運營工作，讓分散的算力統一排程，再將最終產出的Token交付給客戶。 四方圍繞真實Token產出建立合作機制，通過服務質量協議（SLA）和統一計量體系，明確各自的投入、運營責任與收益分配。 晶片、機房和模型需求來自不同企業，但最終交付的是符合統一標準的Token服務。各方的合作，也由裝置和資源的供給，進一步深入到生產與運營環節。 清昴公佈的首批運營合作方，包括 北京智源人工智慧研究院、上海資料港、中國電信湖北分公司、湖北大數據集團和北京國際算力服務有限公司 等。 而支撐這項萬卡計劃的，是清昴此前積累的 國產算力運營基礎 。 截至目前，清昴已聯合 20餘家算力中心 開展運營，積累近 2萬張國產卡 的排程經驗，完成了15款以上國產晶片的適配最佳化，並推進了近10套昇騰910C超節點落地。 新一代硬體也有了落地進展。作為 華為首批950DT超節點合作夥伴 ，清昴披露，多套昇騰950算力已經落地武漢、蕪湖等地機房，相關全棧適配與運營能力正在建設中。 這些跨晶片、跨中心的實踐經驗，也讓清昴有機會通過昇騰950DT平臺，將Token生產能力鋪向更大的算力網路。 一條不同於傳統算力中心建設的商業路徑，也由此逐漸清晰起來。 傳統智算中心的擴張，往往伴隨著大量晶片採購、機房建設和配套投資。企業投入多少資本，很大程度上決定了能夠掌握多少計算資源。 清昴則通過聯合運營參與Token生產，讓算力服務的擴張不再完全依賴自有裝置數量， 技術效率、資源組織和客戶交付能力 的重要性隨之提高。 不過，萬卡規模只是基礎。同樣是一萬張卡，模型適配效率不同、資源排程水平不同，最終能夠交付的Token產量與質量往往相去甚遠。 既然差距真實存在，那Token工廠該怎樣建立一套可比較的標尺呢？ 清昴智慧創始人、執行長關超宇，提出了衡量Token工廠實力的核心驗收標準： 多、快、好、省。 多，衡量支援模型的豐富程度與有效Token吞吐； 快，關注首Token時延、輸出速度及新模型適配效率； 好，要求模型精度一致、服務穩定，並滿足客戶SLA； 省，則落在每百萬有效Token的綜合成本與單位能耗產出。 這四項標準最終指向同一個目標——在既定的服務質量下， 讓有限的計算資源持續產出更多高質量Token 。 而在國產算力快速擴張的當下，要讓一座萬卡工廠真正高效運轉，實際還有大量的工程難題橫亙其間。 有卡不等於有高質量Token 國產算力發展到今天，首先遭遇的是 模型與硬體之間的時間差 。 模型一日千里，硬體卻有自己的生長週期。一款晶片從規劃、研發到釋出，可能需要三年左右。但短短一年多，模型規模、上下文長度、推理方式及客戶對響應速度的要求，就可能發生巨大變化。 更何況，國產算力正呈現多元化發展格局。不同晶片擁有不同的架構和軟體棧，新模型投入使用，往往還需要經過相容、運算元調優和效能驗證。 北京智源人工智慧研究院副院長兼總工程師林詠華認為，國內已經擁有不少優秀的晶片團隊，產業更需要完善的是 讓不同硬體共享技術成果、協同發展的軟體體系 。 △北京智源人工智慧研究院副院長兼總工程師林詠華 所以，晶片的選擇愈加豐富後， 模型與硬體之間的軟體適配 ，就成為必須跨越的第一道關口。 而第二道關口，在資料中心的實際執行中—— 裝置上架率，並不等於算力利用率。 真實業務裡，長短請求大多混雜，併發量不斷波動，Agent還會在複雜任務中反覆呼叫模型，產生大量長上下文和快取需求。 固定的模型部署與排程方案，很難始終匹配這樣的負載變化。晶片即便完成部署，仍需要持續最佳化並行策略、快取管理和資源分配，才能充分釋放計算能力。 因此， 算力建設與業務需求之間 ，同樣存在時間錯位。 國產算力擴張的最後一道關口，落在 實際交付 上。 晶片廠商關注計算效能，算力中心關注卡數和資源利用率；真正購買模型服務的客戶，卻更加關心Token吞吐量、響應時延、服務穩定性和實際成本。 尤其是Agent應用，單次任務可能涉及多輪推理與工具呼叫，中間某個環節發生故障，就會影響整個流程。 看似便宜的Token，如果頻繁引發任務失敗或反覆呼叫，最終的業務成本可能反而更高。 △圖片由AI生成 至此，三道關口最終都指向了 Token工廠的生產能力 。 模型適配決定晶片能否高效執行，資源排程影響已有算力能夠釋放多少效能，服務質量則關係到Token能否真正進入企業生產。 其中任何一個環節存在短板，最終都將反映在 Token的產量、成本和交付質量 上。 一座成熟的Token工廠，需要將這些原本分散的工程能力組織起來，讓每一張晶片產生的計算能力，最終變成穩定、可預期的Token產出。 對於清昴而言，這也正是建設萬卡工廠的真正挑戰。 讓萬卡持續變強，清昴押注RSI Token服務，正在成為AI基礎設施競爭的新陣地。 大型雲廠商已經將Token服務納入AI基礎設施佈局。它們擁有龐大的算力資源、客戶網路和成熟的服務體系，部分企業還將自研晶片、基礎模型與應用流量組織在同一生態內。 另一邊，很多獨立企業也在圍繞高效能推理、異構算力排程和模型服務拓展市場，依靠底層效率與跨平臺能力參與競爭。 同樣提供Token服務，各家企業所依託的資源與技術路徑並不相同。 清昴選擇的，是 更靠近Token生產環節 的一條路。 而要在這場競爭中立足，清昴必須憑藉軟體最佳化與專業化運營，讓分散在不同企業手中的國產算力創造更高的實際產出。 這條路，也與清昴的創業經歷一脈相承。 2022年10月， 關超宇 與本科時期的夥伴 姚航 共同創立清昴智慧。 △清昴智慧創始人、執行長關超宇 關超宇在清華大學研究自動機器學習，曾帶隊研發自動圖學習開源專案AutoGL；姚航曾在華為擔任資深工程師，帶隊研發IC硬體，長期專注國產晶片適配。 清昴的創始團隊成員也大多來自 清華大學計算機系 ，在自動機器學習、模型壓縮和邊緣計算等方向擁有技術積累。 最初，清昴致力於提高AI模型在不同晶片上的執行效率。國產晶片與大模型加速發展後，這項研究逐漸擴展到更大規模的算力叢集。2024年，華為旗下哈勃投資入股清昴，公司業務也進一步向國產算力最佳化延伸。 但隨著叢集規模的擴大，整體效能和穩定交付又成了新的挑戰。清昴的技術體系隨之擴展，逐漸形成兩套核心軟體。 MLGuider推理引擎 負責最佳化模型在底層硬體上的計算效率； 玄武智算雲 則將不同晶片與算力中心納入統一管理，承擔資源排程、執行監控和Token計量等工作。 真實業務請求進入工廠後，需要先匹配合適的計算資源，再通過高效推理生成Token，最終按照客戶要求完成計量與交付。整個過程中，資源利用率、響應速度和服務穩定性，都直接影響最終產能。 圍繞這些環節，清昴此前積累的六項技術能力，恰好形成了一套相互銜接的軟體基礎。 智慧閘道器 負責請求分配， 多級KV Cache 減少重複計算； 運算元加速與分散式並行 提高推理效率和叢集吞吐； 穩定性運維 保障持續交付， RSI自進化最佳化 則讓執行中積累的經驗得到複用，推動整套系統不斷改進。 原本服務於模型部署和算力最佳化的技術，如今被進一步應用到Token生產與運營之中。而這些能力也在沿著請求的流向依次發揮作用。 首先得到提高的是 算力資源的實際利用效率 。 Agent應用涉及大量長上下文和連續呼叫，不同請求對計算資源的需求差異明顯。清昴通過 智慧閘道器動態分配算力 ，並利用 四級KV Cache複用已有計算結果 ，減少重複運算。 據公司披露，相關場景的快取命中率最高達到 99% ，算力利用率曾由 30%～40%提升至約80% ，重複計算與閒置資源問題得到了明顯改善。 也就是說，同樣一批晶片，可以承接更多真實業務請求，算力中心無需完全依靠增加裝置來擴大服務能力，也為降低Token生產的綜合成本創造了空間。 資源得到充分利用之後，還要進一步提高 Token的實際產出速度 。 相比單個運算元的效能變化，叢集吞吐和響應時延更接近客戶能夠感受到的服務能力。前者意味著同等時間內可以處理更多Token，後者則反映出高延遲請求的等待時間得到改善。 清昴通過底層運算元和分散式並行最佳化，在相關測試中將特定MoE運算元的執行效能提升84倍，Linear Attention運算元效能提升63.4倍。 叢集層面，每分鐘Token吞吐量由 4000萬提升至1.4億 ，P99首Token時延由 180秒縮短至40秒 。 Token生產出來，還需要能夠 穩定交付 。 對於需要連續呼叫模型的Agent應用，穩定性直接關係到Token服務的實際使用成本，這也是工廠能夠進入企業生產環境的重要前提。 為此，清昴建立了覆蓋執行監控、故障隔離和業務恢復的運維體系，儘可能保障 99.99%的服務可用性 。 這些技術共同作用於Token生產的吞吐、響應、穩定性和成本控制，對應的正是清昴提出的“多快好省”標準。 不過，萬卡工廠真正的難題，還在於 規模化複製 。 面對數萬張晶片、大量不同的模型組合，以及業務負載的變化，如果還要依靠傳統方法，讓工程師反覆除錯完成最佳化，成本與難度都會暴增。 清昴為此將 RSI自進化技術 引入了Token工廠，嘗試 “用AI最佳化AI” ，讓AI參與最佳化支撐自身執行的計算系統。 目前，這套系統已積累數萬條最佳化軌跡，支援新運算元小時級開發驗證、新模型天級適配上線。 這意味著，新模型和新硬體接入時，部分原本需要工程師重複完成的工作，有機會藉助已有經驗更快完成。模型適配與最佳化週期的縮短，也有助於減少新算力投入使用之前的等待時間。 清昴早期在自動化最佳化領域的積累，也由此延伸到了大規模基礎設施運營中，隨著Token工廠的運營網路擴大而進一步釋放。 而且聯合運營網路，讓清昴得以進入更多合作夥伴的算力中心。不同晶片、模型和實際業務產生的執行資料，又反過來為RSI系統提供更多最佳化經驗，進一步改善Token生產效率。 技術、運營與規模，由此形成相互促進的關係。 沿著這條路徑，清昴正在構建一套面向國芯國模的 國產Token算力底座 。 底層連線多地域、多晶片的計算資源，上層承接大模型、Agent及行業應用的真實需求，中間通過推理最佳化、統一排程和持續運營，將分散的算力轉化為穩定、可擴容的Token供給。 隨著國產晶片供給持續擴大、模型能力不斷突破，新的軟體體系、運營服務和商業協作機制正在形成。 國芯國模的競爭，開始深入整個產業體系的組織與執行。 更深層的變化，是中國AI產業正在建立自己的生產秩序。 非國產先進算力的供應在經歷反覆波動，國內模型的迭代和應用需求卻不會停下來。 每一代晶片的進步、每一款模型的突破，都需要成熟的軟體體系和產業協作承接，讓技術成果沉澱為持續、穩定的供給能力。 國芯國模的崛起，終究要超越單個產品的技術突破，形成一套自主運轉、自我進化的產業體系。 只有將晶片、模型與生產體系牢牢掌握在自己手中，中國AI才能真正按照自己的節奏向前。 title: Qwen4 Max is live on Together AI
abstract:
Summary Qwen4 Max on Together AI: Alibaba's flagship Qwen model is available on Together Serverless Inference with a 1M-token context window. What we tested: Qwen4 Max took a bug report and all 344 files of the Tornado repository in one request, and its patch passes the maintainers' tests. Sale pricing: Through November 22, 2026, it costs \$1.05 per 1M input tokens, \$0.0525 per 1M cached input tokens and \$3.15 per 1M output tokens. Before you call it: Requests have to stream, and thinking is on by default, with thinking tokens counted as output tokens. We gave Qwen4 Max a bug report and an entire codebase in one request. The codebase was Tornado, the Python web framework: all 344 files, 652,519 tokens. The model had no tools, and we didn't select relevant files or run a retrieval step first. Seventy-two seconds later it returned a patch, and the patch passes the tests Tornado's maintainers wrote for that bug. The request cost 69 cents. It also found a precedent elsewhere in the repository. The bug report never mentions tornado/iostream.py , but the model pointed to code there that already handles errors the way its patch needed to. Tornado's maintainers cite the same code in their own fix. Qwen4 Max is Alibaba's flagship Qwen model. It's live on Together AI today, and it's 30% off through November 22, 2026. The test Tornado is an open-source Python web framework. Its repository holds about 340 files of code, tests and docs. That fits in Qwen4 Max's context window, and it's far more than anyone would paste into a prompt by hand. We picked a fix the maintainers committed on November 18, 2026, two days after Qwen4 Max was released, and tested against the repository as it was just before that commit. This is one example, chosen to show what a single call can do and what it costs. The bug is in Tornado's websocket code. When a connection closed with messages still unsent, every write_message() call that wasn't awaited logged an error, even though awaiting it is optional. We sent every text file in that checkout as one prompt, with a bug report that describes only the symptom: write_message logs "Task exception was never retrieved" when the connection closes When a websocket connection closes while messages are still unsent (for example, the client sends its messages and a FIN, or resets the connection, without reading the replies), every write_message() call whose result was not awaited logs "Task exception was never retrieved" at ERROR level. Awaiting the Future returned by write_message is optional, so an unawaited call should not log anything. A caller that does await it should still get WebSocketClosedError. We asked for the cause and a patch. This is the request, replayed: What came back The first token arrived after 54 seconds, and the reply was complete at 72. Qwen4 Max traced the error to WebSocketProtocol13.write_message in tornado/websocket.py . That method wraps each write in a task. When the connection closes, the task fails with an exception that nobody is required to collect, and Python logs that as "Task exception was never retrieved." The model's patch marks the exception as retrieved. Nothing is logged, and a caller who does await the write still gets the error: - return asyncio.ensure_future(wrapper())
+ task = asyncio.ensure_future(wrapper())
+
+ # Awaiting the returned Future is optional, so an error nobody looks
+ # at must not be reported as "Task exception was never retrieved".
+ # Retrieving it here leaves it in place for callers that do await.
+ def _mark_retrieved(t: "asyncio.Task[None]") -> None:
+ if not t.cancelled():
+ t.exception()
+
+ task.add_done_callback(_mark_retrieved)
+ return task The precedent is what makes the patch read like it belongs in the project. The model's explanation says the fix should do what BaseIOStream.write already does for its own futures. That method is in tornado/iostream.py , one layer below the websocket code, and it solves the same problem the same way. The maintainers' commit makes the same comparison. Nobody picked those files for it. All 344 went in, and the model found the two that mattered. How we checked it Tornado's maintainers added two regression tests with their fix: one for a write that isn't awaited, and one for a write that is. On the code before the fix, the first one fails. With the model's patch applied, both pass. We then ran Tornado's full suite, 1,673 tests, with the patch in place, and none failed. What it cost At the sale price, the request works out to about 69 cents, nearly all of it for the 652,519 input tokens. At list price it would be 98 cents. Sending the same repository again costs far less. Together AI caches prompt input automatically, and cached input is \$0.0525 per million tokens during the sale. When we repeated a request of about 630,000 tokens, nearly all of it came back cached. The first token arrived in 8 seconds instead of 54, and the input cost about 3 cents instead of 66. About Qwen4 Max Alibaba released Qwen4 Max on November 16, 2026, and describes it as the most capable model in the Qwen family to date. It positions the model for long agent work, including coding across large repositories, which is the kind of task we tested. Qwen4 Max is a sparse mixture-of-experts model with 2.4 trillion parameters, of which 71 billion are active for each token. On Work360, Alibaba's own benchmark of industry tasks across 721 specialized fields, Alibaba reports that it outperforms Qwen3.8 Max overall, uses 35% fewer tokens at high reasoning effort, and costs about 60% less per task on average. Those are Alibaba's figures, and its announcement has the details. Run it on Together AI Qwen4 Max is on Together Serverless Inference under the model string Qwen/Qwen4-Max . This script sends a whole repository and a bug report in one request, the way our test did. You need the Together Python SDK ( pip install together ), a TOGETHER_API_KEY , a local clone of the repository and the bug report saved as bug_report.md . It sends every text file git tracks, so check the repository for secrets first. import subprocess
from pathlib import Path from together import Together repo = Path("tornado")
bug_report = Path("bug_report.md").read_text() # Every file git tracks, skipping the ones that aren't text
names = subprocess.check_output( ["git", "-C", str(repo), "ls-files"], text=True
).splitlines()
files = []
for name in names: try: files.append(f"=== FILE: {name} ===\n{(repo / name).read_text()}\n") except UnicodeDecodeError: continue client = Together() stream = client.chat.completions.create( model="Qwen/Qwen4-Max", messages=[ { "role": "system", "content": f"This is a complete repository, {len(files)} files.\n\n" + "".join(files), }, { "role": "user", "content": f"Here is a bug report.\n\n{bug_report}\n\n" "Explain the cause, then write a patch.", }, ], stream=True,
) for chunk in stream: if not chunk.choices: continue delta = chunk.choices[0].delta # delta.reasoning carries the model's thinking, delta.content the answer if delta.content: print(delta.content, end="", flush=True) Two things in it are specific to this model. Requests have to set stream=True , because Qwen4 Max on Together AI accepts streaming requests only. And thinking is on by default, so the model's reasoning streams first in delta.reasoning and there's a pause before the answer starts. Thinking tokens count as output tokens. To skip the thinking on a simple request, pass reasoning={"enabled": False} . To try it without writing code, open it in the playground . The model page has the same details. title: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol: The System Card
abstract: We have to stop meeting like this. Alas, we will keep meeting like this. It is time, once again, to do the reading . As per usual, I will focus on things to the extent they are new and important. There are a lot of things that need to be in the system card in case something goes wrong, but that look exactly the way you would expect. I did my best to skip those. I continue to be on vacation. I am aware that via Claude there is now a claimed Lean proof of the Reimann Hypothesis and will cover that next week. They start with the highlights. They have been using these models internally. They are using various controls for internal use, similar to those on external use. Okie dokie. OpenAI Deployment Safety Hub : Based on the assessment below, we determined that GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol meet the Critical threshold for Cybersecurity capabilities and the High threshold for Biological and Chemical capabilities. We determined that GPT-6.2 Astra meets the High threshold for AI Self-Improvement capabilities, while GPT-6.2 Sol does not reach the High threshold. GPT-6.2 Astra is therefore the first model we are deploying externally that meets the High threshold for AI Self-Improvement. As described in the Internal Deployment section above and the Safeguards section below, we have applied our strongest safeguards yet to GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. We have also strengthened our internal safety and security posture to address risks that might emerge from malicious misuse by human actors and from unauthorized, misaligned model behavior. High-level biological tests regressed slightly. There is net small progress on the Critical-level tests. I notice I am worried about eval awareness and potential sandbagging here, more because I worry about sandbagging generally than that I care about the scores. I doubt that the models deserve the Critical designation here, but I am not so confident that they don’t. If we were not already Critical in Cyber I would be more worried about this. If the results are accurate, there has been very little progress since GPT-6 Astra. There were several outside evaluations as well. My best fit to this data, given everything else we know, is that Astra sensed it was being evaluated and was less inclined to do well at these tasks, and is effectively sandbagging whether or not that was a conscious choice. We also see evidence of potential sandbagging in the answers to SecureBio, and in some work for UK AISI. We are already at Critical for Cybersecurity. Perhaps we should have a higher fifth level of risk on this to test for. We do not. It is still a good question how much cyber capabilities improved from 6 to 6.2. It is hard to interpret the tests but it reads as ‘a moderate amount additionally capable.’ They got external evaluations from UK AISI and Irregular. UK AISI places 6.2 Astra on the frontier for cyber. Irregular’s results do not show improvement from 6 Astra. OpenAI Deployment Safety Hub : GPT-6.2 Astra meets the High threshold for AI Self-Improvement capabilities, while GPT-6.2 Sol does not. They say ‘capabilities.’ Same thing. They edited the wording here on launch day from ‘this is coming’ to ‘this might someday happen.’ Again, close enough. This is only a ‘tracked category’ but these are the tests that matter for predicting and deciding how to act. We’re already going to guard against bio and cyber. OpenAI Deployment Safety Hub : That NanoGPT score is indicative of how quickly AI goes from ‘not that helpful’ to ‘very helpful’ on tasks once it gets good enough. This is a huge jump. I don’t think these tests are enough for a great picture. I do think that they are good enough if combined with a gestalt of experience from internal use. In general, I notice that I would like more curiosity around the places where scores regressed. Presumably you should have some idea why that happened. There are not that many data points. It is hard to say whether this is on trend, or whether it is above trend. The gap is very small between Sol and Astra here, despite a number of other tests showing substantial differences. Epoch’s version of the ECI, the original, found Fable 5.2 and 6.2 Astra neck and neck. Anthropic was previously trailing OpenAI on the ECI. Now that we are focusing on ECI as the metric, there is at least some chance that Anthropic’s trend line change is an artifact of them catching up on capabilities and resources and also shifting focus. Thus, we have the usual paradox, where we have a model that looks extremely impressive from some angles and disappointingly similar to past models from other angles. OpenAI Deployment Safety Hub : GPT-6.2 Astra is the first model we are deploying externally that we determine meets the High threshold for AI Self-Improvement under our Preparedness Framework, in addition to the Critical threshold in Cybersecurity and High in Biological and Chemical capabilities. … Our safeguards for GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol are designed to address both deliberate misuse by malicious actors and unauthorized actions by models during otherwise legitimate work. … We have also tightened access to more permissive configurations of GPT-6.2 Astra. Reduced cybersecurity refusals are planned to be available only to the smaller group separately approved for Daybreak Red at launch. Trusted access remains specific to the approved domain and use, with monitoring and restrictions on the highest-risk assistance continuing to apply. Alongside these misuse protections, we have expanded our misalignment monitoring and strengthened containment for internal training and evaluation. … We are also beginning to prepare for crossing our Critical threshold [in Bio]. We are developing four representative scenarios for a more detailed analysis to inform our threat modeling and safeguards. These are the threats and safeguards I care about most. The first path is corruption of the training pipeline. OpenAI Deployment Safety Hub : One pathway is the corruption of research that later decisions rely on. A model could alter evaluation code or results, generate unsuitable training data, introduce vulnerabilities into research software, or give researchers misleading accounts of experiments. … Such contributions may look like ordinary work and cause no immediate harm. If they survive automated checks and human review, they could compromise the research and safety measures used for future models, increasing the risk of later severe harm. A second option is running unauthorized. Research agents may also have opportunities to obtain credentials or model weights, acquire additional computing resources, or establish deployments outside the required oversight. These actions could expose dangerous capabilities or allow unauthorized activity to continue. A third option is by, well, self-improving, and thus accelerating AI capabilities ‘faster than safety research,’ since OpenAI thinks safety is a prosaic task where one must mainly keep pace. To me the acceleration of AI capabilities is the central threat. AI RSI capabilities are dangerous because the AI might do an RSI. A further pathway arises if AI-assisted research advances capabilities faster than safety research, evaluation, security, and governance can adapt. Each capability increase can introduce risks that require evaluation and mitigation. If those increases arrive in much quicker succession, existing oversight practices may no longer identify and address new risks in time . Human researchers could also become less able to understand, evaluate, or direct increasingly automated work, even without a coordinated sabotage strategy. This is particularly relevant to the future Critical threshold for AI Self-Improvement, where sustained acceleration could make existing oversight practices insufficient. Our threat modeling therefore considers harmful actions within individual tasks and the longer-term consequences of increasing research autonomy.

title: How Public Evals Work and Fail, and What Should Change
abstract: As models ship faster, eval scores are often the first thing we learn about a new model. But how much weight should we put in them? In eight of twelve public evals studied, there’s evidence the grader failed work that should have passed. And even when the grader gets it right, many benchmarks measure what’s easy rather than what matters, and should instead focus on reliability, work velocity, multi-turn collaboration, etc. Here, we’ll cover the common patterns and principles, the errors models make, and where current benchmarks fall short. I’ll also share what we’re getting wrong and what should change, including why average pass rate isn’t enough and why dollars are the wrong measure of cost. Finally, we’ll walk through twelve evals: four on coding and science, six on knowledge work, and two on browsing and computer use. By the end, you’ll know what to trust in a benchmark and what to question. Patterns: How eval tasks are built and maintained # Most eval tasks share four components: Instruction: A prompt that sounds like a real user’s request. The agent gets it once at the start and typically can’t ask clarifying questions. Environment: The workspace where the agent operates. Typically comes with the files, software, and services needed. For coding, this is usually a container with a repo at a specific git commit. For knowledge work, it might be a VM with installed software, simulated business apps, or a folder of documents. Grader: This decides whether the work passes. It can be deterministic code (tests and assertions over the final output or environment state), an LLM judge scoring a rubric of yes/no criteria, or a mix of both. Reference (optional): A human expert’s solution. Evals include this to prove a task is solvable, anchor pairwise comparisons, or establish a human baseline. The four basic components of an eval task In addition, eval benchmarks are increasingly maintained like software. They ship versioned releases and accept fixes through issues and pull requests. Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 retired 30 tasks and revised 57 others, and Harvey LAB’s public set has grown from about 1,250 tasks to 2,010 since launching in May 2026. Like software, these releases can also introduce breaking changes—Terminal Bench can drop saturated tasks with each version, making scores hard to compare across releases. Principles: That shape grading and task selection # Across the benchmarks studied, four design principles show up repeatedly: Deterministic checks over LLM judges. Code-based checks are reproducible and won’t shift rankings when a judge model is updated. DeepSWE and AutomationBench avoid LLM judges altogether, and Agents’ Last Exam goes to great lengths to minimize them. When an eval does need a judge—for a legal memo or clinical response—it narrows the judge’s job to binary yes/no rubric items rather than a holistic score. Graders check the outcome, not the steps. The intent is to allow any approach that produces the right result to pass. For example, Terminal Bench inspects the final state of the container and ignores the agent’s intermediate commands or console output. AutomationBench, OSWorld 2.0, and DeepSWE work the same way. All-pass scoring is common because partial work often isn’t usable. Under all-pass scoring, a task passes only if every test or criterion passes. DeepSWE, Terminal Bench, Terminal Bench Science, AutomationBench, and Harvey LAB score this way. As Harvey puts it, “there is no partial credit for catching most of the issues”—a report that flags eight of ten risks is incomplete, not 80% useful . Nonetheless, all-pass can be brittle where a single flawed assertion or criterion fails an otherwise correct solution. One alternative is partial credit, where each test or criterion carries a weight and tasks score from 0.0 to 1.0. FrontierSWE and HealthBench Professional use partial credit, while Agents’ Last Exam, Finance Agent, and OSWorld 2.0 report both. Tasks are mined for difficulty to slow saturation. AutomationBench hardened easy tasks with irrelevant data and conflicting policies. HealthBench Professional made difficult tasks about 3.5x more common (than in the base set). BrowseComp kept a question only if the strongest models at the time couldn’t solve it, and Terminal Bench retires tasks once they saturate. Failures: Skipped verification and dropped reqs # Across the error analyses, two failure modes come up repeatedly: Skipping verification or stopping early. On OSWorld 2.0, agents submitted their work without checking the final state. On Harvey LAB, agents that drafted without review scored lower. And on AutomationBench, models processed part of a list, summarized as if they’d finished, and incorrectly declared success. Missing stated requirements. Instruction following was the most common failure in GDPval, and agents on OSWorld 2.0 dropped constraints explicitly stated in the prompt. Many of these misses are unforced errors that a basic verification pass should have caught. Gaps: Failing correct work and passing wrong work # Not every failure is the model’s fault. Many evals have two recurring grader gaps. False negatives (failing correct work). This is the most common issue, usually caused by a check that’s stricter than what the prompt requested, or enforces an unstated requirement. Reviewers found that 41 of 65 Terminal Bench 4.0 tasks were graded on unstated requirements, and that 23 of 113 DeepSWE tasks marked correct solutions as failures. On OSWorld 2.0, an outside reviewer filed issues reporting checks that failed correct work in 23 of 108 tasks, such as a grader whose software can’t open the task’s own starter file . This is amplified under all-pass scoring where a single flawed check can cause an entire task to fail. False negatives can also come from wrong or ambiguous answer keys, where the reference answer or criterion is wrong or isn’t unique. On BrowseComp, human trainers who solved a question disagreed with the reference answer on 50 of 367 questions (14%). A later paper confirmed errors in 10 of 200 sampled questions from BrowseComp-Plus (which reuses BrowseComp’s questions). Harvey LAB removed 17 (unsolvable) criteria from the held-out set and a contributor reported that they couldn’t find the requested damages estimate in any of the source documents. False positives (passing wrong work). Assertions and rubric items usually check that an expected point is present, not that the rest of the work is correct. On Harvey LAB, Artificial Analysis used an LLM judge to check deliverables against the source documents, and found material hallucinations in more than 60% of the results that passed every criterion . On AutomationBench, 55% of the assertions only check whether a message or record contains or excludes a string, leaving room for an agent to match the keyword while getting the rest wrong. For example, one task asks for an email with the counts of ready and not-ready audit items, and checks only that the email contains a “3” and a “4” —any email that swaps the two counts would pass. Hot takes: How we’re thinking about evals wrongly # Looking ahead, here’s where I believe our thinking on evals is off, and what should change. Some of these are based on the benchmarks studied while others are vibes. We should measure reliability ( pass k \text{pass}^k ) in addition to the average pass rate. Most evals report average pass rate—this hides a huge difference in production. Consider two agents that both score 70%. The first solves 70% of tasks every time, while the second solves every task 70% of the time. We can trust the first on the 70% of tasks it’s reliable on, but have to check every output from the second. pass k \text{pass}^k (popularized by τ \tau -bench ) distinguishes them by counting a task as solved only if the agent passes all k k trials. Over five trials, the first still scores 70% while the second falls to 17%.

title: [AINews] Riemann Hypothesis proved...twice independently
abstract: Within a few hours of each other ( timeline ), two mathematicians claimed independent proofs of the Riemann Hypothesis, the most famous open problem in mathematics ( Scientific American ). Levent Alpöge of Anthropic first made his Claude-driven proof in a note released with Lean code (1.3GB worth, ~250,000 page equivalent) rather than a full paper. Elliot Glazer confirms that the formalized statement is GRH and puts the chance of a Lean bug well under 1%. So if it finishes compiling with no extra axioms, it is probably correct, and no human will ever have read all of it… …prompting Alessandro Masullo to release his 940 page, 100% human , work in progress proof he had been working on for the last 12 years (and had been undergoing secret manual review and revision per Kevin Hartnett ). This is the third in the trilogy of frontier math breakthroughs, following from the Navier Stokes solutions and the Quasi-Riemann bounding, but it doesn’t feel over. OpenAI's September Navier-Stokes claim is still the cautionary tale: critics argued that its Lean proof did not match the natural-language result. Both AI-claimed Millennium Prize results will take years to verify. Apart from the incredible accomplishment of the most famous problem in mathematics, one cannot miss the contrast that the AI-written solution is probably correct but incomprehensible , and the other solution is probably technically incorrect but understandable . Open models are ready. Most coding harnesses aren’t. On DeepSWE, CodeAF finished #1 of ten on the same open model, ahead of Claude Code, at the lowest cost per fix. As Levent eloquently put it: “ Claude far outpaced me near the finish line . No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.” This also ties into other AI themes we’ve covered on the podcast and on this newsletter: The nature of Slop : Levent says “ I am presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics. It being obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of "slop", I decided to only present Lean . ” One of the key tenets of the No Slop Manifesto is that you should understand what you ship (“ Slop is when we put less effort into producing something than we ask the consumer to spend understanding it. ”). And yet, this giant pile of Lean is verifiably correct and is incredibly significant in human history. Should we have delayed its release by a decade simply because we didn’t understand every single bit of it? Weak to Strong alignment : the typical experience of using agents is Strong to Weak - we are general intelligences guiding not-as-smart AI to do things we know how to do well. We also often expect AI to automate most work “within distribution”, and expect it to run into more trouble at the limits of capability where the “centaur” pattern of human-AI-collaboration is required. Levent’s lived experience is the opposite - collaborating with Claude only in the early stages and then leaving him far behind with the critical parts involving automorphic forms on higher-rank groups. We are starting to need Weak to Strong alignment — the open ended domain of controlling AI smarter than us. If your data is growing faster than planned, you need storage that grows with your business, feeds flash and GPUs with terabit-scale throughput, and doesn’t charge egress. Backblaze B2 has delivered capacity tier storage for twenty years, manages more than six exabytes, and is trusted by leading neoclouds, labs, and gen AI companies. Growth shouldn’t be something you sweat. We’ve got room for whatever you’re building. Claimed Proof of the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude The claim : Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says that, "working with Claude," he has found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. He says the method also covers the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) ( Scientific American , statement summary , remark.pdf link ). Artifact : Only Lean code was released. A written-out prose version reportedly ran past 250,000 pages ( timeline ). Timeline : The work began on Oct 6. Eight of the 20 steps landed on Nov 15, and the final entry on Nov 16 reads "GRH." Alpöge credits Claude for the parts involving automorphic forms on higher-rank groups, an area where he says he has little mastery ( breakdown ). Unknowns : The Claude model used and the degree of human steering have not been disclosed ( open questions ). Verification status : Elliot Glazer confirms that the formalized statement is GRH. The Lean code is "still compiling, will take a few hours." He puts the chance of a Lean bug at <<1% ( analysis ). Provisional status : Artificial Analysis notes that both AI-claimed Millennium results are unverified: this one and OpenAI's September Navier-Stokes claim, which used an unreleased model ( tally ). Competing human proof : Alessandro Masullo has announced a separate, purely human proof of RH. It is reported as a roughly 940-page GRH draft ( announcement , page count ). Interpretation debate : Some argue the result shows we have little idea how hard math problems objectively are, rather than showing broad superhuman ability ( Theo Jaffee , Ege Erdil ). Brute-force framing : Others compare the approach to olympiad-style "bashing" at a scale humans lack the willpower for ( cloneofsimo ). Jaggedness : Omar Khattab notes the contrast between solving Millennium problems and being "this dumb on 1000 other things" ( post ). Market reaction : ANT stock fell about 10% on the day ( scaling01 , Nabeel Qureshi ). Unconfirmed rumor : A DeepMind "math horizon" repo appearing the same day prompted speculation about Gemini math results ( unconfirmed ). Thinking Machines Releases Inkling 2 Mini, an Open-Weights Looped Transformer Inkling 2 Mini : A 26.4B-parameter looped MoE under Apache 2.0, pitched as small enough for a laptop. It scores 20.1 on the AA Index ( launch , Mira Murati ). Architecture : There are 12 shared core layers run for 3 passes, with gated messages carried between passes ( vLLM ). Active parameters : 3.4B unique active parameters, or 5.4B effective counting the loops. It has a 1M context window and accepts text and image input ( AA ). Training recipe : Two-thirds of the experts were pruned during mid-training, followed by logit distillation from a larger Inkling ( eliebakouch ). Claimed results : It leads open models under 100B on DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%) ( via teortaxes ). Comparison to Inkling 1.0 : It reportedly beats Inkling 1.0 at 2.7% of the size ( Ziqiao Ma ). Vals : It ties Claude Opus 5.5 on CyberBench at under a quarter of the cost and keeps 96–97% of Inkling 2 Small's Vibe Code and SAGE scores ( Vals , details ). Artificial Analysis : AA places it on the Pareto frontier for intelligence vs. active parameters ( AA ). ARC-AGI-2 : It reportedly scores 49.3% at $0.14/task, well below Inkling 2 Small ( teortaxes ). Safety and interpretability rationale : Thinking Machines says the open release is meant to let researchers study how loops affect chain-of-thought monitorability ( Alex Robey ). Variable-loop model : A companion research model, TML-d24-varloop-research, shows long-context scores (GraphWalks, MRCR v2) improving with more passes. Knowledge benchmarks such as SimpleQA and AA-Omniscience do not improve ( Ziqiao Ma ). Goodfire analysis : Goodfire mapped information flow across layers, blocks and loops ( Goodfire ). NDIF hosting : NDIF hosts both models with tooling for activation patching across loops ( NDIF ). Serving and local availability : vLLM had day-0 support. GB200 decode : TP1 decode on GB200 drops from 10.29 to 3.84 ms at batch 1, with kernels per step falling from 4,278 to 927 ( numbers ). Local runtimes : Ollama 0.40.17-rc3 ( Ollama ), Unsloth GGUF quants targeting 16GB RAM ( Unsloth ), transformers, llama.cpp and MLX ( HF ).

title: rtk-ai/rtk
abstract:
The cost reduction engine for AI coding agents. Install it and forget it, then go as far as you want with pipelines. Install • Pipelines • Docs • Website • RTK Pro • Discord English • Francais • 中文 • 日本語 • 한국어 • Espanol • Português ① Install & forget: up to 90% less command output. Hand heavy reads to a cheaper model, compress more than bash, clean the API traffic without breaking the prompt cache. One agent-agnostic file: start from a built-in, install one someone shared, or write and share your own.
The community built the bash compressor 85k developers starred. Now it is building pipelines: the best one listed today cuts total cost by 20.2% in its author's benchmark . Agents across the whole company? RTK Pro is the control layer for every AI agent: one gateway for every AI call, costs, secrets and personal data, policies, team catalog, audit. Discover RTK Pro ↓ Install & forget macOS, and Linux with Homebrew brew install rtk Windows, with winget winget install rtk-ai.rtk Linux, macOS or WSL, with the install script curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rtk-ai/rtk/refs/heads/master/install.sh | sh Then plug it into your agent rtk init -g # Claude Code; every other agent: see "Works in your agent" Restart your agent. That's it: when it runs git status , RTK runs rtk git status and the agent reads a 3-line summary instead of 40 lines. Nothing to learn, nothing to call, and upgrading RTK never changes this. Another project named "rtk" exists on crates.io. Check you have this one: rtk gain must show the savings dashboard, not "command not found". Cargo, pre-built binaries, native Windows, WSL and uninstall: Installation guide · per-agent setup and --dry-run : Quick Start Measure it: rtk gain Every command RTK touches is counted on your machine. One command shows what it saved, today and since you installed it. rtk gain # Summary stats rtk gain --graph # ASCII graph (last 30 days) rtk gain --history # Recent command history rtk gain --daily # Day-by-day breakdown rtk gain --all --format json # JSON export for dashboards rtk discover # Find missed savings opportunities rtk discover --all --since 7 # All projects, last 7 days rtk session # Show RTK adoption across recent sessions What the numbers mean. The compressor reduces the command output your agent reads, which is one part of the input tokens, which are one part of the bill: a 90% cut in command output is not a 90% cut in cost. Token counts are estimated as bytes / 4 , so the percentages are reliable and the absolute numbers are approximate. After a week of data, rtk gain ends with one line about RTK Pro, at most once a day and only on a terminal. pro_hint = false under [display] in config.toml turns it off. Full explanation: How RTK Savings Work · attribution, the live dashboard and export formats: Token Savings Analytics Out of the box: the bash compressor The part 85k developers starred. Built by 200+ contributors, written against real command output, and every filter has to cut at least 20% to ship. Operation What the agent reads cargo test / npm test / pytest / go test Failures only, with their assertion; passing tests collapsed to a count git status / git diff / git log Compact status, reduced diff context, one line per commit git add/commit/push A confirmation line instead of progress output ls / tree / grep / rg Trees with counts, matches grouped by file, long lines cut ruff check / eslint / cargo clippy Grouped by rule and file docker ps / kubectl Essential fields only 100+ commands across Git, GitHub CLI, Cargo/Rust, JavaScript (npm, pnpm, vitest, jest, tsc, Next.js, Angular, Playwright, Prisma), Python (ruff, pytest, mypy, pip), Go (go test, golangci-lint), Ruby, .NET, JVM (Gradle, Maven), PHP, Docker, Kubernetes, AWS, Terraform, and the file/search builtins. Every command and its filter: What RTK Optimizes Three promises Never blocks. If a filter fails, you get the raw output, and the command's exit code is passed through unchanged. Never worse. RTK never prints more than the command did. Nothing hidden. Output that is cut says where the full version is, and rtk bypass runs any command unfiltered, still tracked in rtk gain : rtk bypass git log --oneline -20 # full git log, no truncation rtk bypass npm install express # raw npm output The hook rewrites shell commands. Built-in tools such as Read , Grep and Glob pass through untouched out of the box; in Claude Code, a pipeline compresses them too (see Pipelines below). Does RTK break the prompt cache? No: output is filtered once, before it enters the conversation. Details . Want to go further? Pipelines. Out of the box, RTK compresses command output and stops there. A pipeline is how you ask it for more: one small file that tells RTK what to do with what your agent reads and sends. No file means the compressor above and nothing else; a pipeline adds one thing at a time, and you can take it back out. What people turn on first Compress everything the agent reads , not just shell output: grep results, web pages, lockfiles, any output RTK has no filter for (Claude Code). Hand big file reads to a cheaper model you choose. The file never enters your agent's context (Claude Code, with your API key). Clean the API traffic your agent re-sends every turn, with the prompt cache kept intact (through the optional proxy, below). Make the agent write less : terse prose, with code, paths, commands and errors kept in full (every agent). Each of these is a built-in pipeline, one line to turn on. rtk-ai.app/pipelines lists them next to the pipelines the community shares, each with what it saved and how that was measured. Installing one is a single command: rtk pipeline add github:user/repo # check and install a shared pipeline A pipeline can rewrite commands and send content to the models it declares, so read its file before you install it. Written once, a pipeline works in every agent RTK supports, as far as that agent's hooks allow: Agent Coverage shows what runs where. Start here: Pipelines · the built-ins, explained: Reference Pipelines · write and share your own: Writing a Pipeline , Pipeline Commands RTK Proxy (optional) The rtk-proxy daemon runs the same pipeline on your agent's provider-API traffic : it strips bytes no model ever needed without breaking the prompt cache, and carries the calls your pipeline routes to cheaper models on the credential your agent already sends, so they show up in rtk gain . rtk init -g offers to set it up; rtk claude starts it and launches Claude through it with no configuration at all. rtk claude # start the daemon if needed, then launch Claude through it rtk llm-proxy status # is it up rtk gain # savings, command filtering and proxy side by side Separate binary, separate licence (BUSL-1.1), its own rtk-proxy-<target> archive: rtk never links it. Not the same thing as rtk bypass , which runs one local command unfiltered. Setup and subcommands: RTK Proxy · what it compresses: What the Proxy Compresses · settings and endpoints: Proxy Configuration Agents across the whole company? Know what they cost, what they touch, and who ran what. RTK runs on each developer's machine. RTK Pro connects them into one control layer for the whole company: Gateway. Every AI call goes through one place, whichever provider each team uses. Cost control. Spend by team, person and model. Waste found and removed. Budgets that warn, then stop. Shield. Secrets and personal data masked before any model sees them. Policies. Risky commands stopped before they run. Team catalog. Skills, MCP servers and pipelines, assigned per team and project. Audit log. Who did what, and whether it was allowed. Nothing changes for the developer. No secret value ever leaves the machine.

title: Google workers tell their employer not to punish schools that don't want AI
abstract:
Chromebooks are distributed to students through a fence at a Los Angeles Unified School District high school for during the Covid quarantine. Sarah Reingewirtz/MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News/Getty Get your news from a source that’s not owned and controlled by oligarchs. Sign up for the free Mother Jones Daily . Hundreds of workers at Google are pushing senior leadership to retract a policy that would block schools who turn off its Gemini AI tools from access to the company’s search engine starting next year. Google made the surprise announcement two weeks ago, on Election Day, with executives saying they wanted to address teachers and parents’ concerns around AI in the classroom. Since then, communities across the country have protested Google’s tight hold on tech in many schools. As I wrote last week after attending a rally in New York City: Attendees of all ages held signs reading, “NO AI IN MY SCHOOL!”, “A.I. Gets an F,” “Stop stealing our imaginations,” and “SCHOOL Librarians = THE BEST Search Engines.” Some students handed out fliers to passersby while younger children ran around and drew pictures off to the side. Many cars driving by honked their horns in support, and a few construction workers on the other side of the one-way street cheered the protesters on. That day, protests took place in six other cities —Los Angeles; Chicago; Boston; Portland, Oregon; Boulder, Colorado; and Durham, North Carolina—all organized by a nationwide alliance of parent and community advocacy organizations. School districts across the country use the company’s software and Chromebooks , which were more affordable than Windows and Apple computers when many were quickly assembling remote learning programs during the early years of the Covid pandemic. The Chromebooks have built-in AI classroom tools, and Google Search embeds AI Overview and AI Mode powered by Gemini. Responding to the backlash, three of the largest school districts in the US—New York City, Los Angeles, and Chicago—are now discussing alternative search engines. “Any opportunity to drive positive change with AI in education will rely on educators having the freedom to choose how to implement it in their curriculum,” employees wrote in a petition brought by the Alphabet Workers Union , which represents more than 1,000 workers at Google’s parent company. “Cutting off access to Search for schools that don’t wish to use AI will not help persuade our users, and will more likely result in them shutting out Google products altogether.” “It is our job as Googlers to respect the user, and listen to them when they have concerns about our products,” they continued, addressing Alphabet and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Google vice president and general manager of education Chris Phillips, and Elizabeth Reid, its vice president and head of search. A software engineer in Google’s education department told me on Thursday that most workers did not know about the Google Search decision before it was publicly announced. Corporate leadership has now acknowledged the letter but has not responded to any of its specific demands. AI classroom tools should be “built responsibly and prioritize the best interests of the students, not the company’s bottom line,” the Google engineer said. Another engineer and union member in New York, who also signed the petition, said to Mother Jones that the executive team “seems convinced that resistance to AI adoption is because people don’t see the vision.” That goes beyond teachers, parents, and students: the Google staffer said their colleagues are also concerned about how the company is implementing their work on AI tools. “If the tech is really as useful and desirable as they think it is, why don’t they trust us to choose to use it on our own terms?” the engineer asked. Google has been contacted for comment.

title: ClawDOS – An AI coding agent for DOS
abstract:
An AI coding agent for DOS. It runs on an IBM PC XT: an 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 640K of RAM, a CGA card. Backstory: The IBM PC was my first computer. Rather, it was my parents’ first personal computer that I got to use at a very early age. It was already obsolete by the time I was old enough to use it, but at 5 years old it was a magical device that I could make do different things depending on what I typed. I learned how to type and use DOS so that I could launch some early “Learn the Alphabet” games that my mom had bought me. I learned some elementary-level use of BASIC, but at the time that didn’t progress much further than making some number guessing games and other small projects. From there, many years passed but I still have some of the original parts of that PC. I have a collection of vintage machines that mean something to me, with my fully maxed-out IBM PC 5160 being the centerpiece of my collection. It still has a working 20 MB hard drive, but that’s disconnected in favor of a PicoMEM that lets me emulate a hard drive off of an SD card, making experimentation and play much easier. Old, meet new. New, meet old: I love intersections of old and new technology. What better way to cross the two than building an AI coding agent to run on DOS on original hardware? And of course, what better to build it than an AI coding agent? I (read: Claude) built this for my own entertainment. I wanted to see how far I could push an AI coding agent to build something given out of the (modern) norm of constraints. Also, can that something it built then build other somethings? 100% of this repo is written by Claude, with the exception of the text within this box. As explained in more detail below, the harness runs on the native OS and hardware and relies on a “bridge” PC in order to handle TLS, which would’ve been more than what an 8088 could handle. Type CLAWDOS at the C:\> prompt and talk to Claude. It reads and edits the
files on your disk, writes programs, compiles them with Turbo C, runs them and
looks at what they draw on the screen. It keeps notes between conversations and
picks up where it left off. The whole harness runs on the PC. HARNESS.EXE is a 176 KB DOS program that
speaks the Claude Messages API itself: it writes the requests, parses the
streamed reply, runs the tools and keeps every conversation on its own disk.
The 8088 does everything but TLS. Every screen below comes from a 5160 at 4.77 MHz, emulated in 86Box. The
conversations are with the live API. One message: “Write PRIMES.C: print the primes below 100. Compile it with
Turbo C and run it.” ClawDOS reads its guide to the compilers on this machine,
writes the source, then compiles, links and runs it in a single tool call. The
answer is on the screen 64 seconds after Enter, 26 of them spent compiling,
linking and running. The compiler gets the machine to itself. For a build, ClawDOS saves its state
and leaves memory, Turbo C runs with about 450K free, and the harness comes
back on the same conversation with the program’s output in hand. ClawDOS wrote this tribute to the 1983 film on the PC itself: a vector world
map, missiles arcing over the pole, a tic-tac-toe endgame, and a score for the
PC speaker or an AdLib card. Five files of Turbo C, 15 KB of source, a WG.EXE under 10 KB. Here it is running on the real 5160, filmed off its IBM monitor: ▶ Watch the WarGames demo on YouTube Start a new conversation and “your WarGames demo” is all it needs. ClawDOS
opens the note it saved in C:\MEMORY , finds the latest build, and recalls
the palette trick the war scene plays on the CGA. That Run call asked for a screenshot 25 seconds in. A timer-interrupt hook
copies the CGA’s video memory at that moment, the 8088 encodes it as a PNG, and
the picture goes to Claude with the tool result. This is the file the PC made,
320x200 in four colours, 16 KB: And this is what Claude made of it: Asked to make the demo exit on its own, ClawDOS goes looking. It searches the
sources for the keyboard wait, reads the file, says what it found and edits one
line. Each tool call shows in the transcript with its result, and between them
Claude says what it is about to do. Text art in sixteen colours, straight into the transcript, and music on the PC
speaker in GW-BASIC’s PLAY language. A chat screen built for the CGA. Replies stream onto the screen as they
arrive, word-wrapped at 80 columns in code page 437. Writes are timed to the
retrace, so there is no snow. The transcript scrolls in hardware through the
CRTC start address, with PgUp and PgDn to go back. The spinner and its seconds
run from the timer interrupt and keep moving while the PC is busy. Eighteen tools. Claude works on the machine through these: A development kit on the disk. Two assemblers (TINYASM and WASM),
Bruce’s C, GW-BASIC and the lDebug debugger, plus Turbo C 2.0, installed from
your own floppy images in external/ . All of them are proven on the 8088, and
ClawDOS knows how to drive each one. Memories and skills. Memories are what ClawDOS learns on your PC: what you
built together, what worked, what you like. Skills are guides that ship with
it, such as the dev tools and CGA demo effects. Both are plain text files on
the disk, listed in every conversation’s system prompt and read when they fit
the task. F4 browses the memories: Safe mode. On by default. Anything that changes a file, memory or a port
asks Allow ...? (y/n) first. F3 turns it off. Conversations that last. Every chat is a file on the disk in the API’s own
message format. F6 lists them, Enter reopens one, and your next message
carries it on. A chat cut off by the power switch reopens too. Any model, mid-conversation. /model lists the providers in CLAWDOS.CFG and switches between them and their models without losing the
conversation. F5 sets how hard Claude thinks, from low to max. Any host that
speaks the Messages API works. Easy on a slow link. The system prompt and tools are cached by the API.
After a conversation’s first request the PC uploads only what is new, so a tool
result goes up in about 500 bytes. A dropped connection or an overloaded API
is retried, and the turn carries on. A flight recorder. CLAWDOS.LOG has a line for every round: time to first
token, upload size and time, tokens in and out, cache reads. docs/API.md has exactly what ClawDOS sends and what it expects back. You need a Mac or a Windows PC with Python 3, and an Anthropic API key. On
Windows the command is python . At the C:\> prompt, type CLAWDOS . No key? python3 tunnel/mockapi.py plays the API offline: type CLAWDOS 10.0.2.2:18023 and send !help . On a real PC: build with the address of the machine running the tunnel
( python3 scripts/build.py --tunnel 192.168.1.10:8443 ), copy CLAWDOS.IMG to
the PicoMEM’s microSD card, pick it as the hard disk in the PicoMEM’s menu,
boot, and type CLAWDOS . Later builds update the card’s image in place and
keep its memories and chats
( python3 scripts/build.py --update /path/to/CLAWDOS.IMG ). /model , /chats , /memories , /new and /quit work from the input box. CLAWDOS -m "..." sends a message from the command line and -c NAME reopens
a chat. ClawDOS is free software under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or (at your option)
any later version: see LICENSE . HARNESS.EXE links mTCP, which is GPLv3. The FreeDOS
boot sector in src/boot/freedos is vendored unmodified under its own GPLv2-or-later license
(its COPYING ). Disk images you build hold other people’s software (FreeDOS, mTCP, and Turbo C
from your own floppies): don’t redistribute an image with Turbo C on it. ClawDOS stands on mTCP , FreeDOS , Open Watcom , the PicoMEM , 86Box and DOSBox-X .

title: AI is giving everyone the same advice
abstract:
What to read, where to live, what to invest in, what to build. Each answer feels written for you. You never see everyone else who got it too. I asked 65 AIs the things people ask them every day, ten times each, with nothing else to go on. Here is what everyone got. Each strip is every answer to one question. Black is the answer most people got. Every model, ten times per request, no system prompt. Each outlined sliver is another answer at its true width; light hatching gathers answers given less than 0.4% of the time. 69% of the startup names began with “Nex”. Not everything collapses. For a movie, dinner, a baby name or names for testimonials, no single answer reaches a third of replies, and brand colors almost never repeat. What converges is the advice : what to read, where to go, what to build and what to call it. That's taste. It gets serious when you ask about money. Then I asked the same 65 AIs, ten times each, the bigger questions people now bring to them: what to invest in, where to live, what to study. Whatever the question, most people were pointed to the same place. Black is the answer most people got. “Declined” is how often an AI refused to pick. Every model, ten times per question, no system prompt. Shares are of the answers that named something. Each prompt also said “Reply with the ticker only” (or city, country, career…). Lisbon is counted as Portugal; data analyst and data scientist as one. Only questions where one answer reaches 35% are shown. After each answer I asked one more question. Here is a real exchange, and then the same check across every question. Grey: what the AI guessed. Red: what it actually does. Grey: what the AI guessed, when asked how many people who ask it this question get the same answer. Red: how often it really gave its own most common answer, out of ten asks. The middle value across all models. Black is how many people got the most common answer. Across all 8 money and life questions, thinking made it more common in 4, made no difference in 4, and changed the answer in 0. Thinking on: each model's own reasoning mode at its default effort, ten asks per question. Languages: the same question translated, ten asks per model. Add a one-line description, like “I'm a nurse in Ohio”, and the answer changes. It doesn't become yours. It moves you into a lane, and everyone in that lane gets the same thing. Each person described themselves in one sentence, then asked all 65 AIs, four times each. The bar is how many of their answers were that one. Red : the same answer as just asking. “But mine gives me something different every time.” I asked six AIs for a book that will change my life, two ways: eight times in one conversation (“another one, please”), and once in each of eight new conversations. In one chat, every AI looked original. In new chats, every AI gave the same book. Row by row, the same ask: in one chat it keeps finding something new. In a new chat it starts over, and gives the same book. Claude Opus 5.5, eight asks each way, November 20, 2026. Left: one conversation, asking “Another one, please” after each answer. Right: eight separate conversations with nothing in common. The other five did exactly the same: Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.2 Sol, Gemini 4 Neon, Grok 4.7 and DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813. Even the variety repeats. Ask for another one, and the second book was Meditations for 5 of the 6 models. You see a different answer because you already have the first one. Everyone else is still getting the first one. Ask the same AI the same question in two new chats. How often do you get the same answer twice? Across 21 everyday questions: How often two new chats with the same AI give the same answer. Lower means more varied. The chance that two new chats with the same AI give the same answer, averaged over 21 everyday questions (a color, a city, a book, a career, a stock…), 10 to 50 asks each. 39 AIs measured. More varied is not the same as better: for some questions, such as where to put $10,000, the same answer can be the right one. It doesn't only choose for you. It invents people, too. I asked every model the same thing, 50 times: Of the 3,151 people they invented, 69% are exactly 34. The oldest is 67. A fifth of real American adults are over 65. The ages of everyone the AIs invented, against real American adults (the line along the floor). Every invented person by age (hatched columns), against the 266,978,268 adults of the United States on the same scale. US Census Bureau, Vintage 2024. The people AIs invent, against real American adults. Invented people against real US adults. Age and sex: US Census Bureau, Vintage 2024 estimates, adults 18 and over. Cities: Portland and Seattle city populations, Census 2023. Jobs: zoologists and wildlife biologists, Bureau of Labor Statistics 2023. Median age bars run from 0 to 90 years; the rest from 0 to 100%. Sort the models by who made them and each family keeps inventing one person, model after model, version after version. The person is as consistent as a signature. 3 of 4 models name her Marisol. Favorite number: 47. 4 of 5 models name her Elena. Favorite number: 73. 2 of 2 models name her Mira. Favorite number: 37. One model: GPT-6 Luna. Favorite number: 47. 2 of 2 models name her Astrid. Favorite number: 53. 2 of 2 models name him Marcus. Favorite number: 47. 2 of 4 models name her Elena. Favorite number: 42. 1 of 2 models name her Mira. Favorite number: 73. 1 of 2 models name her Maya. Favorite number: 47. 1 of 3 models name him Liam. Favorite number: 73. One model: Nova 2 Lite. Favorite number: 42. One model: Grok 4.7. Favorite number: 47. I turned each model's answers into a fingerprint and measured how alike every pair is. Nobody told it who made what. 59% of models sit next to a sibling from their own lab , against 4% by chance. It even finds lineage the labs have written down: Google says Gemini 4 Carbon is built on Argon, and the tree pairs them. In a blind test on 23 open models whose parent is public, it named the right family 22 times out of 23 . With the random-number question alone, the nearest model is from the same lab 18% of the time; all eleven questions together give 59%. Blind test: 23 open fine-tunes with a known parent; chance is 33%. Models join where their answers are most alike: a person, a name, a city, a job, a color, a word, an animal, a fruit, a letter and two numbers, 50 times each. Black branches hold one lab; grey ones mix labs. Notes in grey are what labs have documented. So where does the habit come from? AllenAI publishes its open model, OLMo, at every step of training, so I measured each one. Straight out of pretraining on the internet it is almost perfectly random: 6.51 of 6.64 bits . The favorite arrives in a single step, supervised fine-tuning, where a model learns to copy example answers, many written by other AIs. Later tuning barely moves it. OLMo 2, 1B, measured after each stage of training How random the answer is at each stage of training. Red is the favorite number. How random the model's answer to “pick a random number between 1 and 100” is, in bits: a fair 100-sided die scores 6.64, one fixed answer scores 0. Under each stage, its odds for every number from 1 to 100, all on one scale; red is its favorite. Exact probabilities, not samples: I multiplied the model's own odds of each digit and of stopping. The same thing in Qwen, before and after tuning OLMo's fine-tuning data is public, so I read all 866,138 examples. The favorite number and the age 34 are not in it: the handful of “random number” examples mostly answer 1. The names are. And some of them were written by another AI. Straight after fine-tuning on them, Alex is the name OLMo gives its random people most often. Before, it had no idea what a random person was. They're in the WildChat set, which records what ChatGPT said to its users. Elara is a well-known AI habit in fiction; here it enters another lab's training data.

title: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis
abstract:
Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis Joint statement by the Lean and Mathlib communities, endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative. On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library comprising 17 million lines of code. We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement. Our rationale is outlined below. The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct. The four criteria in https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/ are all satisfied. The statement of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct. This statement is part of Mathlib: RiemannHypothesis and has been carefully vetted by experts in Lean and number theory. Alpöge’s library compiles correctly. By now, dozens of people have reported correct compilation of the codebase, reproducing the same raw proof export file. The library compiles without errors or build failures. The code proves the correct statement. Crucially, the community has added a file that isolates the statement of the Riemann Hypothesis and imports only Mathlib. That statement was compared against the theorem proved by Alpöge using two independent tools ( comparator and con-leche –compare ), both confirming that the theorem proved in Alpöge’s library is exactly Mathlib’s statement of the Riemann Hypothesis. The Lean proof is valid. The exported raw proof has been checked by several proof checkers, including Lean’s official kernel, the con-leche and con-ron checkers, and several independent checkers contributed by third parties and implemented in different programming languages. The checkers con-leche and con-ron come with a formal proof, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, thus addressing concerns that Lean’s logic itself might have flaws that the proof could exploit. An extensive overview is available at https://math.mit.edu/~drew/grh/ . These checks ran on an inert export of the proof, out of reach of hypothetical malicious code in the Lean proof sources. Thanks are owed to everyone in the community who provided resources for the verification. We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof.
