title: Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as 'biggest breakthrough in decades'
abstract:
A year after starting treatment, 76.6% of patients were alive; usually 40-45 % of patients given chemotherapy alone survive a year. Photograph: Jeff Moore/PA View image in fullscreen A year after starting treatment, 76.6% of patients were alive; usually 40-45 % of patients given chemotherapy alone survive a year. Photograph: Jeff Moore/PA Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as ‘biggest breakthrough in decades’ Cancer undetectable for one in 12 patients in daraxonrasib trial, while nearly all participants’ tumours stopped growing A pill that can shrink and potentially eliminate pancreas tumours is being hailed as the biggest breakthrough treatment for the cancer in decades. In one in 12 of the patients given the drug, daraxonrasib , during a trial, the cancer became undetectable, and the tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 patients. The trial participants had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body. Though doctors have said the pill cannot yet be considered a cure, and they do not know how long it can keep the disease at bay, they have said it is encouraging news because it appears it will offer patients more time, even if it does not cause full remission. ‘The undruggable became druggable’: a gamechanging treatment for the world’s deadliest cancer – podcast Read more Half of all people diagnosed with pancreatic cancer die within three months, and only about 3% of patients survive for five years when the disease spreads to other organs. It has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK and has a similarly poor prognosis globally. Patients were followed for a year and a half during the trial on average and some did not see the cancer return during this period. Longer studies will be conducted to see if any of the cancers can be put into remission. During the trial, tumours stopped growing in 90% of patients, just over 60% of patients had their tumours shrink or disappear, and for about 8% of patients tumours became undetectable on CT scans. A year after starting treatment, 76.6% of patients were alive; usually 40-45% of patients given chemotherapy alone survive a year. Dr Wungki Park, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, who presented the findings, said “this is the closest to cure”, adding that he had never seen so many tumours disappear in patients whose cancer had spread. He presented the findings at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona. “We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival,” he said. FDA gives expedited approval to new groundbreaking pancreatic cancer drug Read more “The median follow-up is 18 months. Just imagine, in an average of 18 months your disease just disappears on the CT scan … that’s closest to complete remission … it’s incredible.” Daraxonrasib is a KRAS inhibitor treatment, which works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations found in most pancreatic cancers. These mutations drive tumour growth. There are hopes the treatment could work for dozens of other cancers because they can have similar mutations. Michelle Mitchell, Cancer Research UK’s chief executive, said more research was needed, but added: “This is the biggest leap forward we’ve seen in decades for pancreatic cancer patients and could offer real hope to people facing one of the deadliest and most difficult-to-treat cancers. “These results raise the exciting possibility that this breakthrough could eventually pave the way for treating other cancers that carry Kras gene mutations. More trials are now needed before this treatment can be assessed for use on the NHS and despite this advance, pancreatic cancer survival is still very low.” Explore more on these topics Pancreas cancer Cancer research Medical research Drugs Health news Share Reuse this content

abstract:
Nov. 20, 2026, 9:20 AM EST / Updated Nov. 20, 2026, 4:37 PM EST By Rob Wile The surging stock market of 2026 capsized Friday, wiping out gains for the year in the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite while the broad S&P 500 and the Dow entered correction territory, meaning they have declined 10% from recent peaks. The dramatic sell-off is raising fresh fears about the viability of the AI investment wave that had powered stocks and economic growth for the first half of the year. Friday’s declines were led by Anthropic, whose blockbuster IPO just 24 hours earlier now feels like a blip after the stock lost 9%, wiping out hundreds of billions in paper wealth and putting shares just a few dollars above the IPO price. Nvidia also dragged markets lower, tumbling about 14% following a Reuters report that regulators are looking into accounting irregularities at the chip giant. With Friday’s losses of 3.7%, the S&P 500’s seven-day losing streak is its worst since the Covid pandemic; the index is now up less than 1% on the year. The Nasdaq finished the day down 5.3%, and the Dow dropped 1.9%. The losses also sully one of the most visible bright points of President Donald Trump’s second term. Amid sticky inflation and frozen housing and jobs markets, U.S. equities were the one part of the economy that appeared resilient. The AI investment boom created seemingly insatiable demand for stocks among investors, minting multiple new trillion-dollar companies in the process. While Friday’s declines were stark, they were not sudden, capping instead a weekslong slide that began in early October as the combination of elevated oil prices , rising interest rates , mounting corporate debt loads , stubborn inflation , supply chain issues and a flagging consumer put increasing pressure on stock prices. The sell-off picked up steam earlier this month in the wake of Democrats’ midterm victories, which raised fears of a slowdown in the tech sector’s data center buildout. Losses accelerated again last week as the scandal erupted involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and advanced chips potentially being diverted to China. “The stock market is going through an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth,” wrote Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners, in a client note. “This has been exacerbated by the Nvidia crisis and the Democratic midterm win, which were a one-two punch for the AI story.” Market information on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) on Friday. Michael Nagle / Bloomberg via Getty Alongside the stock sell-off, investors have increased purchases of U.S. Treasury bonds — a sign that investors are seeking more reliable returns amid signs of weakening growth from higher interest rates and a stalling economy in China. “The pressure is becoming increasingly widespread, and that’s been felt across other asset classes too,” Deutsche Bank managing director Jim Reid wrote in a note to clients Friday. For U.S. households relying on 401(k)s and pension funds for retirement, the downturn is especially unwelcome at a time when inflation continues to prove nettlesome. Kevin Gordon, head of macroeconomic strategy and research at Charles Schwab, told NBC News that markets are feeling particular pressure from an increasingly “hawkish” Federal Reserve that is signaling aggressive rate hikes in the face of unrelenting inflation. “They’re signaling that they want to be aggressive in raising rates,” Gordon said. Combined with a weeks-long downturn among AI and tech stocks, “we have dual forces hitting the market.” A prolonged downturn could begin to cut more deeply into economic growth, he said. “If you have enough of a protracted downturn, which we really haven’t had since 2007-2009 in terms of length and duration, that’s when you’d really start to worry,” he said. title: Vertical Domain Large Language Models: Applications, Challenges, Future Prospects
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become a cornerstone of modern generative artificial intelligence, demonstrating remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks, including machine translation, question answering, and dialogue generation. However, most existing reviews primarily emphasize theoretical foundations and training methodologies, and offer limited insights into real-world application performance and domain-specific deployment patterns. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic literature review following PRISMA guidelines, synthesizing the application of LLMs across diverse vertical domains. The review examines system architectures, technical approaches, and performance benchmarks reported in the literature. In addition, it analyzes core challenges associated with LLM deployment, such as hallucinations, explainability, value alignment, and data quality, along with targeted solutions. Finally, it identifies emerging research opportunities and future directions, contributing to a more coherent, application-oriented understanding of LLM development and impact.

title: DESIGNING AI-RESISTANT TASKS AS A TOOL FOR ASSESSING THE ANALYTICAL AND CRITICAL COMPETENCIES OF FUTURE TEACHERS
abstract: This article provides a theoretical foundation for assessing the analytical and critical competencies of future teachers in the era of generative artificial intelligence. It has been demonstrated that the limited reliability of automated AI-detection tools necessitates a shift from evaluating the final written product to a "process-over-product" diagnostic paradigm, while upholding the principles of academic integrity. Within the structure of an educator's analytical - critical competencies, the cognitive-diagnostic, didactic-design and reflexive-metacognitive components have been distinguished. A didactic model has been developed for designing AI - resistant assignments that focus on higher-order thinking skills, specifically "Analyzing", "Evaluating" and ″Creating″ according to Bloom's Taxonomy. The model incorporates the ″Three Zones ″ framework and utilizes three diagnostic formats: the analysis of contradictory pedagogical cases (Case Study), the cognitive auditing of AI-generated content (Reverse Engineering), and in-person, dialogue-based defense using the Socratic method (Socratic Defense). Furthermore, a criterion - based, multi-level rubric has been proposed comprising verification-analytical, didactic-adaptive, and metacognitive-authorial criteria to objectively assess students' professional agency and critical thinking.

title: canSAR 2026-an update to the public drug discovery knowledgebase.
abstract: canSAR (https://cansar.ai) serves as the world's largest public platform for cancer drug discovery and translational research. It serves as an exploration and hypothesis generation platform for drug discovery through (i) fully integrating large, multidisciplinary data from public resources, as well as bespoke curated data, creating a connected, navigable drug discovery knowledge map; and (ii) applying a suite of machine learning and AI tools to generate novel insights. We share the latest updates to canSAR highlighting growth across all data, enhancements to the predictive algorithms, and continued improvements to the user experience. We leverage our latest open science chemical handling and druggability prediction tools to provide traceable insights. An increased focus of the platform is to provide "in-line" support and guidance to drug discovery exploration. We report the first incarnation of our high-fidelity, agentic-AI-generated, context-specific summaries, which we provide across the website for all human proteins to further aid users in synthesis and distillation of key information.

title: Multilingual Emotion Profiling of Large Language Models Through Literary Texts and Persona Conditioning
abstract: This paper examines whether multilingual prompt-and-text conditions materially alter large language model (LLM) emotion evaluation rather than merely rephrasing the same task. Using OpenRouter as a unified inference layer, we evaluated six contemporary LLMs under three full-language conditions (Japanese, English, and Traditional Chinese), three literary texts, four personas, and three repeated API calls per condition. Each completion rated four emotional dimensions — Interesting, Surprise, Sadness, and Anger — and provided a brief rationale. The design comprised 648 planned evaluations (6 models × 3 languages × 3 texts × 4 personas × 3 trials). The final combined dataset contained 648 valid records, comprising 631 original records and 17 replacement records obtained under a repair amendment registered after the main run and before the patch run. Descriptive summaries and preregistered ordinary least squares analyses with HC3 robust standard errors showed that text content was a major driver of scores, especially for Sadness and Anger. Simultaneously, model-language interactions were significant for all four emotions, indicating that the effect of the language condition varied substantially across models. English yielded the highest mean Interesting, Surprise, and Sadness scores, whereas Japanese yielded the highest mean Anger score. However, these aggregate patterns mask the strong model-specific contrasts. The findings show that multilingual literary evaluation is shaped by both the text itself and the model processing of its translation. This study contributes a multilingual literary emotion benchmark, a preregistered and repair-aware evaluation pipeline, and evidence that multilingual conditions are substantive experimental factors for LLM emotion profiling.
